title: Rhamondre Stevenson working to return sooner than expected
summary: As the New England Patriots took the field for a walkthrough at the FC Bayern Munich Training Ground on Thursday, running back Rhamondre Stevenson was spotted working off to the side. Stevenson missed Wednesday’s practice in Foxboro with a knee injury that was initially reported to cause him to miss some time. His presence on […]
full_text: As the New England Patriots took the field for a walkthrough at the FC Bayern Munich Training Ground on Thursday, running back Rhamondre Stevenson was spotted working off to the side. Stevenson missed Wednesday’s practice in Foxboro with a knee injury that was initially reported to cause him to miss some time. His presence on the field in Germany, however, offers some optimism that the veteran running back could make a quicker-than-expected return for Sunday’s matchup against the Detroit Lions. “I think that just speaks to, first off, the media not really knowing 100% what they’re talking about a lot of the time,” quarterback Drake Maye said of Stevenson’s return. “And just a guy that wants to be out there, wants to be back for his team and we’re in the midst of trying to make a make a run here and win a big one before the bye. “This is a time for players, a lot of the players on this team that are trying to get out there, play with their teammates and knowing that he’s a great player and can help us out.” Stevenson initially suffered the injury late in the third quarter of Sunday’s 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers after being brought down following a six-yard reception. Reports indicated that Stevenson suffered a knee tendon issue near the back of his knee and while the injury was not expected to require surgery, he could miss the next few weeks. Stevenson, however, was upgraded to a limited participant Thursday which leaves open the possibility of a quicker return. “He’s a dawg, man,” wide receiver DeMario Douglas said. “I know some people that probably be like, ‘Man, I ain’t even going to try’, you but his situation, man, I be talking to him [and he’s] like, ‘I’m going to try. I’m going to do what I can do.’ He’s working, he’s getting better. So, when the time comes, I know he’s working to get better.” Stevenson’s potential return would be a significant boost for a Patriots offense that has dealt with several injuries this season. He has been one of New England’s most dependable players, logging 65% of the team’s offensive snaps while piling up more than 650 total yards and four touchdowns. His contributions in pass protection have also earned consistent praise from teammates and coaches. Potentially without Stevenson and with No. 2 running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness) already ruled out, the Patriots would be left with Corey Kiner and Lan Larison at running back. Terrell Jennings is also an option on the practice squad. Offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels made sure to note Stevenson’s presence in Germany while also expressing confidence in whoever the team rolls out against the Lions on Sunday. “Anytime you lose players like that, you feel it because he’s such a valuable part of everything you do,” McDaniels said. “But why we have a lot of guys that are taking reps in practice. We’ve had a lot of guys doing that all year long. They know what to do. It might not be the same volume of experience that certainly Rhamondre has, but we got a lot of guys in that room that we have confidence in… And Rhamondre is here too.”

title: Patriots have ‘all the belief in the world’ in Christian Gonzalez
summary: The Green Bay Packers had their way with the New England Patriots secondary in Week 9, and one player more than any other was in the spotlight afterwards. Being the closest defender on multiple big plays, Christian Gonzalez was the poster boy for his team’s 45-27 defeat. Despite the performance, however, the Patriots are not […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers had their way with the New England Patriots secondary in Week 9, and one player more than any other was in the spotlight afterwards. Being the closest defender on multiple big plays, Christian Gonzalez was the poster boy for his team’s 45-27 defeat. Despite the performance, however, the Patriots are not hitting the panic button. Instead, their belief in the 24-year-old remains unshaken. “Obviously, Christian had a couple of plays that he’d definitely want back,“ said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr ahead of Thursday’s practice in Munich. “But there are some things that fans don’t see or people don’t see that might not be on Christian, but he happens to be around the ball. And sometimes the blame comes with that. “But we know what Christian’s capable of and we have all the support and belief in him in the world.” According to charting by Next Gen Stats, the Patriots’ No. 1 cornerback became the first defender since at least 2018 to give up 80-plus receiving yards to two different players in one game against the Packers. Overall, the Patriots defense allowed Green Bay’s receiving duo of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden to beat them for a combined 17 catches for 335 yards and a pair of touchdowns. With a Detroit Lions team on the dock more than capable of putting pressure on a defense itself, the Patriots and Gonzalez in particular will need a quick turnaround. According to Kuhr, however, the start was encouraging. “I don’t want to do any predictions or anything like that, but I thought we had a really good day of practice yesterday,“ he said. “There was good energy. There was good execution. There was improvement in communication, some connection in the back end it was exciting to see. There was some good energy out there. I think the guys were excited to get back to work, like, ‘Let’s get this thing right.’”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots vs. Lions: Who has the edge in Week 10?
summary: The New England Patriots had a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad day last Sunday against the Green Bay Packers. Unfortunately for them, they might have to wait a bit longer for a reprieve. Their upcoming opponent, after all, is another one of those pesky NFC North teams. After losses to the Bears and Packers, […]
full_text: The New England Patriots had a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad day last Sunday against the Green Bay Packers. Unfortunately for them, they might have to wait a bit longer for a reprieve. Their upcoming opponent, after all, is another one of those pesky NFC North teams. After losses to the Bears and Packers, the Patriots are now taking on the Detroit Lions on the road. Far out on the road, that is: the two teams will play one another in Munich. How the travel element will impact the game is anybody’s guess. Looking at the different units in a vacuum, however, we can see why the Lions entered Week 10 as the betting favorites . Passing game Patriots pass offense vs. Lions pass defense: Last week’s loss against the Packers once again showed that the Patriots’ biggest offensive issue is their inability to hold onto the football, and it starts with Drake Maye: the third-year quarterback’s three interceptions put the team on the road to defeat. A repeat performance could be disastrous again, but there is reason for optimism. The Lions are a middle-of-the-road team in interceptions, and generally have been less competitive in coverage than Green Bay: they are ranked only 27th in the league in EPA per dropback (0.178). Obviously, their ability to rush the passer is a concern especially against an offensive line that will once again field a new starting five , but if New England can give Maye time in the pocket he should be able to find openings both with his arm and — going against a defense allowing 8.5 yards per scramble — with his legs. | Edge: Patriots Patriots pass defense vs. Lions pass offense: The Packers had their way with the Patriots pass defense last week, with just two players — Christian Watson and Matthew Golden — accounting for 335 yards and two touchdowns. Granted, Green Bay’s passing offense is the most explosive in the NFL, but the Lions’ combination of Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams is capable of exploiting any coverage mishaps or other insufficiencies in the New England backend as well. Add the fact that the Lions offensive line has been very good in pass blocking so far, and even more pressure will be on a secondary that was relentlessly beaten deep last week. While a repeat performance might not be on the schedule this week, until Christian Gonzalez and company show they can bounce back we cannot trust the unit to deliver against another talented opponent. | Edge: Lions Patriots fans, join the game-day huddle! Follow every snap and discuss every decision with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Connect through our live game chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Running game Patriots rushing offense vs. Lions run defense: The Lions defense has had its issues this year, but stopping the run is not particularly high up the list: from a statistical perspective, this is a fairly average unit ranked 13th in EPA per run (-0.115) and 17th in yards per attempt (4.1). While that is not exactly earth-shattering, there a two reasons we are giving the edge to the designated home team in this one. Not only have the Lions shown some significant improvement over the last month and are ranked fourth in run defense since Week 6, the Patriots are also entering the matchup potentially missing their top two running backs and, as mentioned above, facing more questions along the offensive line. | Edge: Lions Patriots run defense vs. Lions rushing offense: The Patriots run defense has rebounded nicely from a relatively rough start to the season, and is ranked fourth in the NFL in EPA per run over the last four weeks (-0.232). However, it might be facing its toughest challenge to date this week. Standout running back Jahmyr Gibbs is one of the NFL’s most productive players, and entering Week 10 with 177 rushing attempts for 847 yards and nine touchdowns to his name. His 55 first downs on the ground, meanwhile, are the most in the league. The Patriots need to bring their A-game to prevent him from going over 100 scrimmage yards for a seventh time in nine games this year, but we are not so sure about their ability to do that. | Edge: Lions Special teams Even though they lost their regular punt returner, Tom Kennedy, to a knee injury earlier in the year and are now relying on career journeyman and ex-Patriot DeAndre Carter, in that particular area, Detroit still has one of the top overall special teams units in the NFL. The Patriots, on the other hand, have been uneven both in the form of kicker Andy Borregales and, more recently, their kickoff coverage. The law of averages favors the Lions, and so do we. | Edge: Lions Coaching The Patriots coaching staff didn’t suddenly forget how to coach last week, but it also would be naive to think Mike Vrabel’s crew does not deserve any blame either. Like the team itself, its coaches are therefore also in the spotlight this week. That means not just X’s and O’s, but also preventing pre-snap penalties and communication lapses from happening on both sides of the ball. The same is true for making in-game adjustments and being ready for Detroit to try to exploit the issues that plagued the team last Sunday. | Edge: Lions Verdict On paper, things are not looking particularly pretty for the Patriots. That’s what happens when you get blown out in your most recent game and looked as vulnerable on defense as you have in multiple years. Of course, that does not mean the Patriots cannot still travel back to the United States with a victory in their carry-on luggage. However, it goes without saying that it takes a significant improvement on both sides of the ball to put themselves in a winning position. And if the Packers game is any indication, that improvement coming is far from a guarantee.

title: Mack Hollins happy with Patriots’ response after post-game challenge
summary: The New England Patriots were, unsurprisingly, not happy with the performance they put forward last Sunday against the Green Bay Packers. No player verbalized that more clearly than wide receiver Mack Hollins, who put a challenge to his teammates. “If you’re not ready to come to work Tuesday and Wednesday and get on that plane […]
full_text: The New England Patriots were, unsurprisingly, not happy with the performance they put forward last Sunday against the Green Bay Packers. No player verbalized that more clearly than wide receiver Mack Hollins, who put a challenge to his teammates. “If you’re not ready to come to work Tuesday and Wednesday and get on that plane and work all this week, you’re probably not meant for this team,” he said. “If there are guys on this team that are OK with that, I’m sure there are 31 other teams they can go to and maybe they can live like that. But we’re trying to get stuff done about this week.” So, with the smoke having settled on the 45-27 defeat, how does Hollins feel about the state of the Patriots? It appears better. Talking to the media on Wednesday, before the team’s flight to Germany for its upcoming international game with the Detroit Lions, he added further context to his prior comments and along the way praised the team’s response to its fourth loss of the season. “I think it’s good,” the 33-year-old said. “We’re excited for another opportunity, and I think the guys are focused on the ‘one week at a time’ mentality, which is a good thing. You’re trying to reach too far ahead or too far behind you, it’s hard to know where your feet are.” Hollins was not the only member of the organization to highlight the Patriots’ work ethic and mental toughness this week. Head coach Mike Vrabel did as well, effectively echoing what the wideout said on Sunday. And even with some time having passed, Hollins stood by every word he said. “If you come after that game and said, ‘We did enough, it’s not my fault,’ you’re not able to look in the mirror and say, ‘I can get better.’ It’s more of that than guys aren’t working or guys aren’t doing things,” he explained. “If you get this result and you’re OK with it, and you’re like, ‘I don’t need to come to practice next week and come to work, and I’d rather be somewhere where I can just relax and not do anything,’ this isn’t the place for you. I always stand by that, because I don’t want to play with guys that are like that. I don’t think we have guys like that, because, like we’ve said, we all we are, we all we need. The guys that are here, they come to play. Is the result always want we want? Hell, no. But do you continue to push that and get better? Yes.”

(Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With another win, the New Orleans Saints continue to drop in the draft order, landing pick 12. Here are two prospects that could be selected at this pick: OT Zeroue Williams I wanted to start with the offensive line and have a fun (not really) conversation. RT Taliese Fuaga has only been disappointing this season, and although I’m blaming the coaching staff for that, they could still be in charge for 2027. If that is the case, and Cesar Ruiz is no longer the starting RG, the tackle could be a target for the Saints. Fuaga was always projected to be a better guard, and the Saints could try to move him to RG while getting a new rookie in at RT. Besides Jordan Seaton at the top of the draft, Utah tackle Zeroue Williams would be a primary option. He’s 6-foot-8, has exceptional length, and moves really well. The main issue for the Saints is that he is a LT, but that would be a challenge they would be willing to take on, even if it’s risky. If a new staff is here in 2027, I doubt tackle would be an option. EDGE Devan Thompkins A significant riser throughout the year, Alabama EDGE Devan Thompkins could be the selection at pick 12. He’s 6-foot-5, 3oo lbs, very athletic, has standout strength, and has been productive this season. What makes him special is his versatility. He is the perfect 3-4 DE, but can easily fit in as a DT or EDGE in a 4-3 alignment. If Brandon Staley is still in New Orleans, Thompkins could be the perfect player to pair with Chase Young and Carl Granderson. If there is a new staff, Thompkins would still be an excellent pick for New Orleans and could be the future at EDGE for the Saints.

title: NFL Picks Week 10: When Everybody’s First… Nobody Is
summary: The New Orleans Saints host the Carolina Panthers this Sunday with first place in the NFC South on the line, for one week anyway. We can all honestly admit that we are in a continuing five-year loop of the NFC South being an absolutely terrible division. Since 2022, no NFC South Champion has ended the season with […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints host the Carolina Panthers this Sunday with first place in the NFC South on the line, for one week anyway. We can all honestly admit that we are in a continuing five-year loop of the NFC South being an absolutely terrible division. Since 2022, no NFC South Champion has ended the season with less than seven losses, and this season should certainly keep that sad distinction intact. This season could easily see the division champ sport double-digit losses. As it stands, New Orleans and Carolina, at 3-5 respectively, are playing for sole possession of first place, but there is still a lot of season to go, and Sunday’s winner will still have Tampa Bay and Atlanta to contend with as well. This may very well feel like the consolation prize division, but a title is a title, and the home Wild Card game that is awarded to the winner will be gladly taken all the same. Let’s take a look at this and all of the exciting Week 10 action in the NFL. Last week I went 14-1! I told you so : Saints over Browns! What do I know : Patriots over Packers? *** WEEK 10 Thursday, November 12th – Thursday Night Football Commanders(2-5-1) at Giants(5-2-1) The last time these two met, it ended in a tie. This time, New York gets the win and all but wins the NFC (L)East. New York wins 27-21. Pick: Giants *** Sunday, November 15th – Very Early Game Patriots(5-4) at* Lions(6-2) – Munich, Germany Detroit gets a fifth-consecutive win, with a scrappy effort in Germany against the Pats, who are still stinging from last week’s beating against the Pack. Detroit wins 20-14. Pick: Lions *** Sunday, November 15th – Early Games Chiefs(6-2) at Falcons(3-6) Kansas City rebounded from their two-game skid with a dominant performance last week, and they will continue to roll here against the floundering Falcons. Kansas City wins 21-13. Pick: Chiefs *** Texans(3-5) at Browns(5-4) Following a dominant road win last week, Houston will get another here, over the overrated Browns in Cleveland. Houston wins 35-24. Pick: Texans *** Vikings(6-2) at Packers(6-3) – Game of the Week After an effort that set offensive football back to the Stone Age on Monday Night, Minnesota broke open the emergency glass to brink Kirk Cousins back to the Twin Cities. This NFC North clash for first place will be a slugfest, but Cousins and company will find a way to win. Minnesota wins 20-16. Pick: Vikings *** Dolphins(1-7) at Colts(2-7) Indy is currently on a five-game losing streak, but they get just what they need to stop the slide, a matchup with Miami. Indianapolis wins 24-9. Pick: Colts *** Bills(7-1) at Jets(2-7) Buffalo’s fantastic season will continue its trajectory with an impressive win over the Jets. Buffalo wins 33-9. Pick: Bills *** Jaguars(6-2) at Titans(1-7) The re-tooled Jags will dominate the Titans in Tennessee. Jacksonville wins 33-6. Pick: Jaguars *** Panthers(3-5) at Saints(3-5) Someway, somehow, the Saints find themselves battling for the NFC South lead, and of all the teams they should face for that distinction, Carolina might just be the ideal opponent, as Kellen Moore and Tyler Shough are undefeated against Bryce Young’s Panthers. This one, just like every single New Orleans Saints victory you’ve watched all season, will come down to the very last play. A Charlie Smyth game-winning field goal on the final play is the difference in this fight to the top of the NFL’s smallest mountain. Saints win 23-20. Pick: Saints *** Sunday, November 15th – Late Games Rams(5-4) at Cardinals(3-6) The Rams will win their fourth-consecutive game by winning against the last team to beat them, Arizona. Los Angeles wins 33-19. Pick: Rams *** Seahawks(5-4) at Raiders(4-5) The Fernando Mendoza era in Las Vegas begins with a tough draw, the reigning Super Bowl Champion Seahawks. The Silver and Black will fight valiently, but ultimately lose. Seattle wins 30-21 Pick: Seahawks *** 49ers(7-1) at Cowboys(4-5) This once-heralded rivalry will continue to be dominated by the Niners, who will win their fifth-straight against Dallas. San Franciso wins 29-16. Pick: 49ers *** Sunday Night Football Steelers(6-2) at Bengals(6-2) Both of these AFC North rivals are riding high on four-game winning streaks, as the winner of this game takes first place in the division. Pittsburgh won the first matchup this season, but Cincy will take the rematch at home. Cincinnati wins 32-24. Pick: Bengals *** Monday, November 16th – Monday Night Football Chargers(0-8) at Ravens(4-5) When this matchup was made during the offseason, it was a no-brainer primetime showdown. Today, not so much. The spiraling Ravens are on a four-game losing streak that can only be snapped by facing the worst team in the NFL, the pitiful Chargers. Baltimore wins 28-13. Pick: Ravens *** There you have it, Week 10 is upon us. Leave us your picks, comments, and insight below!

title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Carolina Panthers
summary: In what is an unconventional matchup for the top spot in the division, the 3-5 Saints will host the 3-5 Panthers on Sunday at noon in the Superdome. The Panthers came out hot to start the season, and it looked like head coach Dave Canales had finally figured out how to get the team to […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 08: Carl Granderson #96 of the New Orleans Saints lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Cleveland Browns at Cesars Superdome on November 8, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images In what is an unconventional matchup for the top spot in the division, the 3-5 Saints will host the 3-5 Panthers on Sunday at noon in the Superdome. The Panthers came out hot to start the season, and it looked like head coach Dave Canales had finally figured out how to get the team to progress around QB Bryce Young. The Panthers were, at one point, 3-2 and sitting in the top spot of the NFC South, and Bryce Young was playing the best football of his NFL career. Since then, the Panthers have lost three straight games, including a blowout loss to the Bucs. The Panthers have still made strides offensively, even though they have been on this losing streak. Currently, the Panthers have the fourth-best passing offense in the NFL, averaging over 261 yards per game. Through the first eight games of the season, Young has thrown for 2,197 yards, 16 TDs, and six INTs. Right now, Young is on pace to finish the season with over 4,500 yards and 34 TDs. Overall, the Panthers are ninth in the NFL in total offense, averaging 362 yards per game, and 11th in scoring, averaging 24.9 points per game. None of these categories are favorable to the Saints’ defense, as they are currently allowing 370.5 total yards per game, 27 points per game, 236 passing yards per game, and 133.9 rushing yards per game, ranking 27th or worse in the NFL in each category. The Panthers have the advantage in both rushing and passing, and they have a true No. 1 receiving threat in Tetairoa McMillan. McMillan has recorded 46 receptions for 625 yards and three TDs so far this season. This could present a matchup problem for the Saints’ cornerbacks. The Saints are currently tied for eighth-most in completions of 20-plus yards allowed, having surrendered 28 through eight games. The big-play opportunities are there for opponents, especially considering that not only are those plays available, but there haven’t been many consequences for attempting them, as the Saints have only four INTs on the season. There are two key areas the Saints can attack. The Carolina offense has been awful at the line of scrimmage when it comes to protecting the QB. The Panthers’ offense has allowed 26 sacks so far this year, averaging 3.25 sacks allowed per game. They have also allowed 104 pressures this year, which is roughly 13 pressures per game. The Saints have the best pass-rushing duo in the NFL in Chase Young and Carl Granderson. The issue with the Saints’ pass rush is that their pressure rate is still a little low, considering how dominant that pair of edge rushers has been. The Saints currently rank just 26th in the league in pressure rate, which means that if it’s not Young or Granderson, the pressure isn’t consistently getting through. Given how poorly the Panthers’ offensive line has performed in pass protection, this game should help improve that number. The other area where the Saints could win is on third down. The Saints are allowing opponents to convert 47.2% of their third-down attempts, but the Panthers are only converting 37.7% of their own third-down attempts. The Saints’ defense will have opportunities to make an impact on this game. They will need to stop the run, contain Bryce Young, and generate pressure with four rushers. If the defense is able to do this, they should be able to limit explosive plays and potentially create turnovers. The Panthers’ offense has given the ball away 12 times this season, and if the Saints can add to that total, they should be able to defend the Dome. How do you feel about this matchup with the Panthers, and do you think the Saints are rounding into a first-place team? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: INTERVIEW: Saints legend Marques Colston on life after football, The Champion Fund and his advice to young athletes
summary: On Tuesday, I had the opportunity to speak with former New Orleans Saints wide receiver Marques Colston, who has successfully transitioned from the football field to the business world. Following a remarkable 10-year NFL career that included a Super Bowl championship, Colston has established himself as an entrepreneur, investor and business leader, with ventures spanning […]
full_text: Former New Orleans Saints wide receiver Marques Colston speaks during a meet and greet with Albany arena football players, coaches and owners at an open house at the Times Union Center on Tuesday, Dec. 5, 2017 in Albany, N.Y. (Photo by Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty Images) On Tuesday, I had the opportunity to speak with former New Orleans Saints wide receiver Marques Colston, who has successfully transitioned from the football field to the business world. Following a remarkable 10-year NFL career that included a Super Bowl championship, Colston has established himself as an entrepreneur, investor and business leader, with ventures spanning professional sports ownership, technology, education and investment management. Today, as the co-founder of The Champion Fund, Colston is helping create new opportunities for athletes and everyday investors to gain ownership stakes in the growing sports industry. During our conversation, we discussed these exciting opportunities, his journey from professional football to entrepreneurship, and his advice for athletes looking to invest in their futures. TH: After a highly successful NFL career with the Saints, what motivated you to get involved in the business side of sports, and what was the thought process behind co-founding The Champion Fund? MC : So for me, the Champion Fund is kind of a culmination of the last 15 years of kind of making my way around the sports ecosystem and the sports business world in a bunch of different seats. As a former athlete, I got one perspective of the investment world. Once I got enough experience and was able to see the other side investment world, it allowed me to see a lot of gaps in the market, just a lot of gaps around how deals are accessed, how you actually get the ability to invest in some of these opportunities. TH: What advice would you give to a young athlete who is thinking about his future and looking to set himself up for success after his football career comes to an end? MC : I would tell them very succinctly to start way before you think you need it. Because what happens is, as you are building your career as an athlete, it’s very easy to kind of get typecast into all of the things that people just assume and presume that athletes are going to do. So, the more that you can figure out what you’re interested in, what you’re curious in, and while you have that sports platform, be curious and continue to explore those things to where once you do transition, whether it’s from high school to college or college to the pros or pros to, I guess you can call it civilian life, you’ve already kind of gotten some reps. You’ve already figured out some of the things that you’re interested in. You’ve crossed some things off the list that you thought you might have been interested in that you’re not. And it just gives you a much smaller universe that you got to navigate. You don’t feel like you got to take on the entire world. TH: What is the biggest lesson you’ve learned from transitioning from being a professional athlete to working on the business side of sports? MC: I would say for me, particularly as a former athlete, that not all access is great access. I think people kind of come into every business opportunity and business dealing with their assumptions of who you are and what you want to get out of a deal. Walking in as a former athlete, a lot of those assumptions are marketing and visibility based. So, for me, the hardest thing has been to really get in the rooms in one way and then kind of maneuver within the room and pivot within the room to get to the place that I ultimately want to get to and not get painted into a corner. TH: Was that something you learned during your playing career, or was it something you discovered after retiring and becoming involved in the sports industry through ownership and entrepreneurship? MC: It’s something that honestly, I continue to learn because, I’ve been out of the game for 11 years now and I still have to navigate some of that. So it’s something that you kind of figure out early on. You’re just excited to be in the rooms. And then as you get more reps and as you get more access, you start to figure out like, yes, I’m in the room, but I’m kind of painted in this corner, signing autographs and taking pictures where I really want to be talking about business. So it’s something that you just continue to learn over time and you just try to figure out how to navigate some of those more misaligned situations, I guess is the easiest way to call them. TH: What would be your biggest piece of advice for someone looking to build an investment portfolio and create long-term security for themselves and their family? MC: I always start with industries and start with things that you have a baseline understanding of how the business works. Because look, investing is hard and it’s the diligence pieces of it, the monitoring of your portfolio, all of those things are difficult. So, you start with industries that you have an understanding of how the business works and you shorten the learning curve there. That’s always been a good approach for me and it’s one of the reasons I ended up back in sports after all these years. I intimately understand sports as a product, intimately understand it from the business side, from running it. So, it shortens the learning curve. And then all of the new iterations of investment kind of becomes the new learning doesn’t feel as it doesn’t feel like, again, like you’re drinking from a fire hose all the time. So, like I always tell people, start in areas that you have a comfort zone, start in areas that you’re curious and let that curiosity kind of take on some of the challenges of learning the different nuances of the industry. TH: You had an incredible 10-year career here in New Orleans, filled with so many memorable moments. Aside from winning Super Bowl XLIV, what stands out as one of your proudest accomplishments or most memorable moments during your time with the Saints? MC: Man, that’s a loaded question. I don’t really tend to think about my career in that way. I think for me, the biggest accomplishment is being a part of the revitalization of New Orleans. Just being down there for the decade that I was there, specifically that first five years, it was, you felt like you were a part of something more than just a football organization. Like you really felt like you were an embedded piece of the community. And to me, that’s the biggest accomplishment. To be able to have a career that had enough staying power, that had enough longevity to really play a role in the organization at that point in time, that to me was the biggest accomplishment. Like the stats are great, the wins are great, the Super Bowl obviously is great, but to be a part of something that was much more than just a result on the field and be a part of revitalization and be a part of kind of re-instilling hope down there and progress down there, that’s the thing that I will always hang my hat on as a part of the Saints. Thank you again to Marques Colston for taking the time to speak with me. Whether he is creating opportunities for athletes, sharing valuable lessons from his own experiences, or helping others build a stronger financial future, Colston continues to make a meaningful difference long after his playing days have ended.

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants sit atop the NFC East. Inside the physical and mental toll of Malik Nabers ’ knee injury | ESPN.com This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place. “Just my attitude,” Nabers said of why he lost himself. “Everybody didn’t know what my mindset was. Just at a loss for words. Didn’t really have a lot of words to say. Didn’t really have, I don’t know, I kind of was empty. Everybody just didn’t know.” There were days when his knee swelled, when it was stiff and didn’t bend. His progress, if it was outlined in a graph, might resemble the stock market during its most volatile month. This sent Nabers into a tailspin. He was fighting himself. “My mind was just all over the place. I didn’t really understand and didn’t really want to communicate well,” he said. “Just didn’t know how to communicate how I was feeling and how things were going because every day it was something new. … So I just didn’t know, I just didn’t really see a process. So he stepped in. https://t.co/K1aM7aopKd pic.twitter.com/xfdlvjTkgF — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 12, 2026 Former Super Bowl champion coach says Giants look like a ‘really urgent group’ | NJ.com “I don’t know that John was ever lacking in intensity or energy, but I’ve certainly seen what he’s infused into that collective,” Tomlin said Wednesday on an NBC call with reporters. “It’s displayed not only in their play, but there was an image the other week of their sideline and how everyone was engaged. There were guys running with the runner along the sideline. “I just think that speaks to what he’s done for them in terms of making them appreciate the urgency required to win and win consistently.” How Arvell Reese quickly turned into unstoppable Giants ‘jackknife’ | New York Post The name “Arvell” means “warrior” in French, “cried over” in Welsh and “Eagle Ruler” in Old Norse. Revisiting the 2026 NFL Draft: Was Arvell Reese a luxury for Giants? Has Francis Mauigoa turned a corner? | CBSSports.com There is a world where Reese is not the best prospect to come out of this draft class, but the odds of him being anything less than just a good player are slim to none. title: 7 winners and 3 losers as Giants fall to Commanders on Thursday Night Football
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants have gotten away with living on the edge all season. Thursday night, they could not as the Washington Commanders scored with :57 remaining to beat the Giants, 24-21. Let’s get to the ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’. Kudos to … Ar’Darius Washington — The veteran safety had what […]
full_text: Isaiah Likely scores a 66-yard touchdown. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants have gotten away with living on the edge all season. Thursday night, they could not as the Washington Commanders scored with :57 remaining to beat the Giants, 24-21. Let’s get to the ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’. Kudos to … Ar’Darius Washington — The veteran safety had what could have been a game-sealing interception of Jayden Daniels at the Washington 46-yard line with 2:15 to play. The offense could not close the game out, however, and the Commanders took advantage of their final opportunity. In his best game as a Giant, Washington also had six tackles and two passes defensed. Jevon Holland — Holland also had a massive interception for the Giants, his fourth of the season and first since Week 3. Holland picked off a Daniels pass for Chig Okonkwo with 5:31 remaining and the Giants holding a 21-17 lead. He was ruled down at the 2-yard line, however, rather than the play being called a touchback. That proved costly as the Giants could not get a first down. J.J. McCarthy — The 23-year-old was a little erratic early in his first start as a Giant at MetLife Stadium. He ended up having an excellent night, 23 of 36 for a career-high 293 passing yards with a touchdown and an interception. McCarthy’s 66-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely with a defender in his face was a tremendous throw. McCarthy throws a SEED to Likely, who does the rest 🔥 WASvsNYG on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/BhOxhfRGdp — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 McCarthy also ran six times for 34 yards, 5.7 yards per carry. Cam Skattebo — The second-year running back had 18 carries for 78 yards (4.3 yards per carry) and 2 touchdowns, including a 13-yard run. He also had 44 yards receiving, giving him 122 total yards. Skattebo also had one highly-publicized sideline incident: Cam Skattebo explains what caused his mid-game puke (via @SNYGiants ) https://t.co/JK1JmyJJYO pic.twitter.com/OjZp0TTT0C — Jomboy Media (@JomboyMedia) November 13, 2026 Skattebo did seem to indicate after the game that he would have liked to have had the ball in his hands more with the Giants trying to close the game out late. Cam Skattebo says the #Giants offense failed to close the game out. He also says he thinks the stadium could be a bit louder when the defense is on the field in critical moments Then he said this about not getting the ball in some key short yardage downs late: “It sucks, and… pic.twitter.com/j5uWaTURHb — Pat Leonard (@PLeonardNYDN) November 13, 2026 Isaiah Likely — The Giants’ outstanding tight end had nine catches on 11 targets for a career-best 127 receiving yards. His 66-yard catch-and-run touchdown on a pass from McCarthy was the longest play of his career. Arvell Reese — The rookie linebacker didn’t have any sacks or true highlight reel plays, but he did make a game-high 13 tackles. Jameis Winston’s hard count — It didn’t work, but you have to love Jameis for trying this. If you listen to nothing else today, at least listen to Jameis Winston's hard count here lmao 😂 pic.twitter.com/F1nr26EN3W — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 Wet Willies to … Dominic Zvada — How long do you think it took GM Joe Schoen to ring Nick Folk’s agent, or start compiling a list for a placekicker workout, after Zvada missed a 33-yard field goal in the first quarter on Thursday night? The Giants lost by three points, and Zvada missed a field goal from extra-point distance. The Giants want to believe the rookie will develop into a quality kicker, but he is now just 17 of 23 (73.9%) and his misses are costing the Giants games. Zvada also had a costly kickoff out of bounds penalty after the Giants’ go-ahead touchdown with 8:13 remaining, putting the ball at the 40-yard line. Theo Johnson — The play below was a third-and-3 at the Commanders’ 46-yard line in the fourth quarter with the Giants trailing 17-14. Great throw on 3rd down. No catch. pic.twitter.com/NrU7Eoai3S — Bobby Skinner (@BobbySkinner_) November 13, 2026 An NFL tight end has to make that catch. Johnson’s inconsistent hands have been an issue since the Giants drafted him in 2024, and they hurt the Giants Thursday night. I will admit I did not like the play call there. Why not run the ball on third down, then go for it on fourth down if you don’t make it? Analytics said the Giants should have gone for it there, anyway. Still, that’s all moot if Johnson just catches the ball. Giants’ four-minute offense — The interceptions by Holland and Washington gave the offense two opportunities to put the game away. The Giants could not get a first down either time. The first time, JWinston’s tush push first down was overturned on replay forcing the Giants to punt from their 11-yard line. The second time, the Giants had third-and-3 at the Washington 39-yard line coming out of the two-minute warning. J.J. McCarthy lost two yards on a designed quarterback run. The Giants actually missed a ton of opportunities to score points, so it wasn’t just the four-minute offense that couldn’t get the job done. CRAZY STAT: #Giants had 6 offensive possessions that crossed midfield and ended with no points scored 3 punts, an interception, a fumble and a missed FG https://t.co/OufAR76gcx — Ryan Dunleavy (@rydunleavy) November 13, 2026 Kwillies to … Jordan Stout — The Giants’ punter is fantastic. On Thursday night, he had punts of 68 and 64 yards. He also had a touchback from the 46-yard line early in the fourth quarter, and shanked a 12-yard punt from the 41-yard line that put the Commanders at their own 29-yard line with 1:46 to play. Three plays later, the Commanders scored the game-winning touchdown.

title: 4 things we learned from the Giants’ 24-21 loss to the Commanders
summary: Well, the New York Giants have still not beaten Jayden Daniels, and they put forth an embarrassing performance in front of their home fans in losing to the Washington Commanders, 24-21. This was a game the Giants had in the palm of their hands and let slip away. Let’s mention a few things they did […]
full_text: Well, the New York Giants have still not beaten Jayden Daniels, and they put forth an embarrassing performance in front of their home fans in losing to the Washington Commanders, 24-21. This was a game the Giants had in the palm of their hands and let slip away. Let’s mention a few things they did wrong and right in this game. John Harbaugh (and his offensive staff) are too conservative Harbaugh has done a lot right in leading the Giants to first place in the NFC East. But sometimes I feel that he is not honest about the team he has. Harbaugh wants to be the coach of a dominating running team. The Giants as currently constituted are not that, yet he (and Matt Nagy) play it conservatively until they can’t, and then they still do anyway. He decides not to change place kickers, but after Dominic Zvada misses a 32-yard chip shot, that’s it for the night, and when the Giants get down to the 32-yard line, they punt on fourth down rather than attempting a 50-yard field goal. Nonetheless, the Giants manage to take a 21-17 lead late in the game. The Commanders drive and Jayden Daniels takes an end zone shot and is intercepted on a beautiful play by Jevon Holland. Unfortunately the INT occurs at the 2-yard line, putting the Giant in a hole. Two Cam Skattebo running plays later, it’s third-and-1, and Harbaugh tries another Jameis Winston sneak to get the first and fails. Eventually, after a ridiculous attempt to draw Washington offside (as if they would really believe he’d try to run a play that deep in his own territory with the game on the line), and an unnecessary delay of game penalty resulting from that, Jordan Stout bails him out once again with a 68-yard punt that backs Washington up to its own 37. The Giants get the ball back at the Washington 46 with 2:15 left, and Harbaugh tries to run out the clock as much as he can and make the Commanders use their timeouts while doing so. The problem is that he doesn’t have Derrick Henry, Ronnie Stanley, and Tyler Linderbaum on this team. He has one of the worst run blocking offensive lines in the NFL and a good but not great running back. Skattebo gains 7 of the 10 yards he needs to effectively close out the game on first and second down, and then with third-and-3, rather than have J.J. McCarthy pass to get the first down and seal the win, the Giants dial up another of those J.J. RPOs that I think have not yet worked even once. McCarthy loses yards, the Giants punt from the Washington 39 (that’s two punts from inside the opponent’s 40), and predictably, Jayden Daniels drives the Commanders downfield for the winning score. Playing to win can mean running the ball with a lead when you have a dominant run game. When you don’t have a dominant running the game, running the ball just serves to take a little time off the clock and make your opponent use a time out or two. When your opponent is a quarterback as dangerous as Jayden Daniels and your running game is mediocre at best, the play should be to be aggressive. Will Deonte Banks ever learn to turn his head? Banks has thrived under Dennard Wilson after looking like he was on his way out the door. Yet he continuous to have one serious weakness. Last week in Philadelphia, he got beaten on a deep route, never turned his head to locate the ball, and ran into the receiver, a flag that will be thrown every time. That led to an Eagles TD. Tonight he did exactly the same thing again. With 1:46 left and the Giants still ahead, Daniels threw deep to Treylon Burks and again, Banks ran into him. It was an iffy call, since it appeared that Burks at the same time was pulling Banks toward him, but when you don’t turn your head, you’re always going to be the one that gets flagged. That was one of two terrible defensive plays that cost the Giants the game. The other came on the very next play and was the game winner for Washington. Stefon Diggs, out of the slot, ran right down the middle and was wide open for the winning TD. Why was he so open? Because Dennard Wilson had Dru Phillips in the slot covering him. What? I love Dru’s hustle, his run defense, and in general his play around the line of scrimmage. But I think we are pretty sure, in his third year, that Dru cannot cover receivers of any kind downfield, much less an elite receiver like Diggs. With 1:06 left in the game the Commanders trailing, and third down, I think we can be pretty sure the play is not going to be a run or a short pass. What is Phillips doing on the field in that situation? Ar’Darius Washington becomes a Giant There were bright spots for the Giants’ defense in this game. Jevon Holland made a great interception on a pass to Chig Okonkwo that would have been the TD that put the Commanders ahead in the fourth quarter. The other Giants defensive player who stood out, though, was Ar’Darius Washington. I was intrigued when the Giants signed him, a low-key smart kind of move that doesn’t make headlines but winds up being a good decision. Up to now my intrigue had not been justified. Washington wasn’t playing a lot and wasn’t doing anything notable when he was in there. Tonight, though, he made two great defensive plays. In the fourth quarter, with the Giants still trailing 17-14, Washington drove to the Giants’ 33 and were on the verge of putting the game away. Then on third and 4, Daniels completed a pass to Okonkwo that looked as if it would go for a first down, but Washington tackled him two yards short. Then on fourth down, the Commanders went for it, and Washington broke up the pass to Stefon Diggs. Three plays and one beautiful J.J. McCarthy 66-yard TD pass to Isaiah Likely later, the Giants had the lead: Back to back GREAT plays by Ar'Darius Washington!!! Giants ball pic.twitter.com/bfO9D6FUZl — Bobby Skinner (@BobbySkinner_) November 13, 2026 Can anyone explain to me why Dru was in the game rather than Ar’Darius on Washington’s winning TD drive? It takes J.J. McCarthy a little while to warm up Last week I started to worry about J.J. McCarthy. He came out of the gate slowly against the Eagles and it wasn’t until later in the game that he warmed up a bit. Eventually he wound up having a pretty good game, but in fact it was Jameis Winston who led the Giants on the TD drive that turned the game. Tonight it looked to me as if J.J. was having similar problems. If his first read wasn’t open, he didn’t seem to be moving on to his next read and finding answers. He did eventually get the Giants’ offense going in the second quarter, leading them on a 16-play, 72-yard TD drive to put the Giants ahead 7-3, but that drive was all rushes, short passes, and J.J. scrambles and keepers. Finally in the third quarter, McCarthy started to show some of the things that made him a high first round pick and allowed him to excite Giants fans in the New Orleans and Houston games. The Giants got the ball at the Washington 46 after a punt, and McCarthy layered a beautiful pass over the first level of pass defenders to Malachi Fields to the 30. That drive ended in a Skattebo TD that put the Giants head 14-10. Then later in the third quarter, after Daniels had driven the Commanders to a TD and a 17-14 lead, McCarthy led the Giants on a 73-yard TD drive to put them ahead 21-17. The key play on that drive was a 37-yard pass play to Malik Nabers, again layered over the first level of defenders, to get the Giants down to the Washington 36. McCarthy completed a 16-yard pass to Malachi Fields after that and then another short one to Nabers, who fumbled (this is becoming an increasing problem for him). In the end, McCarthy completed 23 of 36 for 293 yards. He did have an interception, but overall it was a pretty good performance. Ever since the Giants acquired him, I have been looking for signs of why Kevin O’Connell was willing to give up on him so quickly and for so little when the Vikings didn’t have an obvious alternative on their roster. My all-too-early impression is that he is having difficulty deciphering defenses early on in games…

full_text: Cam Skattebo running with the ball Thursday night. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants suffered a heartbreaking 24-21 home loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. The game was sealed with 34 seconds remaining, when J.J. McCarthy threw an interception on third-and-10. The turnover came after New York’s defense had forced two fourth-quarter interceptions from Jayden Daniels while the Giants held the lead. However, the offense failed to capitalize on either takeaway, going three-and-out on both ensuing possessions and allowing Washington to remain within striking distance — and they struck on a quick slant that led to a Stefon Diggs 32-yard touchdown pass to seize the lead; Tae Banks and Dru Phillips collided, eliminating both players’ ability to make the tackle. The Giants allowed the Commanders to hang around. The offense could not pick up first downs on crucial short-yardage situations; Malik Nabers fumbled the football in the red zone, and Dominic Zvada missed a 33-yard field goal. It was a frustrating loss that allowed the Commanders to stay relevant in the division, while giving them the tiebreaker over the Giants. Here are the immediate positional grades for the Giants. Quarterback J.J. McCarthy finished 23 of 36 for 293 yards with a touchdown and an interception. He was sacked once and rushed for 34 yards, including some impressive runs. McCarthy was hit on his interception, which was too high and short, allowing Rasual Douglas to undercut the throw. McCarthy had a lot of first reads, and the Giants seemed to use a lot more shotgun, spread, lighter packages than usual. He had some impressive throws, but there is offense is still being left out on the field. Grade: B Running back Cam Skattebo averaged 4.3 yards per carry ( 18 attempts, 78 yards ) for a pair of touchdowns with three catches for 44 yards, including a 34-yard catch-and-run that was creatively delivered to Skattebo by McCarthy. It was his backfield again. Skattebo found cut-back lanes and was the energy of the offense, while also adding some key blitz pickups. Devin Singletary had just one carry for three yards and he missed an early blitz pickup for McCarthy. Grade: B+ Wide receiver Malik Nabers caught just five passes for 44 yards. The Giants were trying to get him the ball short, but there wasn’t much space or success, and then the deep shot in the fourth quarter was intercepted. Nabers did, though, secure a 37-yard pass up the sideline. Nabers also had a costly fumble in the red zone. Malachi Fields continues to make plays when his number is called. He secured three passes for 62 yards on four targets. Darnell Mooney caught two passes for eight yards on five targets. Jalin Hyatt played a few snaps in the first quarter and continues to be a track star for the Giants, running wind sprints. Grade: B- Tight end Isaiah Likely caught nine of 11 targets for 127 yards and a touchdown, including a 66-yard catch-and-run touchdown. Likely continues to be one of the most valuable free agent signings in recent memory — excellent bang for the buck. Theo Johnson caught one pass for eight yards and dropped a well-placed third-down pass on a deep corner route. Johnson continues to drop passes when his number is called, which isn’t surprising, but I won’t let that affect the position grade too much given Likely’s performance. Grade: B+ Offensive line The Giants were firing off the ball better than they have been most of the season, but Washington made some crucial plays in short-yardage situations. The pass blocking was fine. Grade: B Defensive line Washington was bottled up for much of the game on the ground. Richaad White had a couple of solid runs, including an 18-yarder; he finished with 47 yards on 11 carries. Austin Ekeler had 26 yards on nine carries, and Jayden Daniels had 28 yards on 11 carries. The defensive line, overall, was bottling up the run, with great plays by D.J. Reader. Shebly Harris also came up clutch with a big STOP at the line of scrimmage and a sack. Grade: A- Edge Abdul Carter continues to be the player opposing offenses circle. He received a lot of attention and drew an important holding call. He also had a tackle for a loss and a quarterback hit. Kayvon Thiboeaux had eight tackles in the game and was hobbled in the fourth quarter; he continues to do the gritty work that is sometimes thankless. Trace Ford and Dawuane Smoot each had a tackle. Grade: B Linebacker Arvell Reese and Micah McFadden were both FLYING around the field, making a collective 23 tackles between them; the former had 13, and the latter had 10. Both players are assets when blitzing and pressuring the quarterback, but Washington was so quick to get the football out that it negated Dennard Wilson’s five-to-six-man pressure packages. Both linebackers played well, though. Grade: A Cornerback For the most part, the Giants’ starting outside cornerbacks covered the Washington wide receivers. Jayden Daniels finished 23 of 33 for 249 yards with three touchdowns. Two of the touchdowns were surrendered by the safeties; the other was by Dru Phillips, who was beaten badly on a slant route by Stefon Diggs. Phillips is who he is as a player in coverage; he is inconsistent with discipline and technique. Tae Banks took a fourth-quarter defensive pass interference penalty that advanced the ball 33 yards with less than two minutes left. Other than that, though, Banks was solid, and so was Greg Newsome II. Banks also had a pass deflected. Grade: B+ Safeties The Giants safeties made two impressive interceptions in the fourth quarter that SHOULD have sealed the victory for the Giants. Jevon Holland intercepted a wheel route in the red zone, and Ar’Darius Washington came away with a pick on an out route on the next Washington drive. Somehow the Giants’ offense couldn’t get a first down. Nevertheless, the Giants’ safeties were impressive, despite surrendering two touchdowns in man coverage: one to Holland and the other to Jason Pinnock. Grade: A- Special teams Terrible. Don’t get me wrong, Jordan Stout had a few excellent punts, but the 12-yard punt in the fourth quarter after the Giants’ second three-and-out was when it became apparent that the Giants were going to blow this game. SIDE NOTE: It was perhaps the worst three-play sequence in recent memory — beating James Hudson’s three-penalty outing from Week 1 of last season: first, the Giants call a read-sweep on third-and-3 where McCarthy is tackled for a loss by Sonny Styles; then, with 1:54 left in the game, up by four, Stout punts the football 12 yards to the Washington 29-yard line, and THEN Tae Banks committed a 33-yard pass interference — ABYSMAL! Back to the special teams. Dominic Zvada missed a 33-yard field goal on the Giants’ second drive. New York’s offense showed life on their first two drives, and they came away with ZERO points, including a missed field goal that Ed could have made. It’s inexcusable at this point. Grade: D-

title: Fantasy Football 2026: Week 10 preview — Start/sit and more
summary: Welcome to Week 10. The 18-Week NFL season is at its halfway point, and the trade deadline has passed. Most fantasy leagues have five weeks left before the playoffs start. Crunch time is here. Six teams switched to a different quarterback in Week 9. It’s one week later and five more new QBs are expected […]
full_text: Golden child | Getty Images Welcome to Week 10. The 18-Week NFL season is at its halfway point, and the trade deadline has passed. Most fantasy leagues have five weeks left before the playoffs start. Crunch time is here. Six teams switched to a different quarterback in Week 9. It’s one week later and five more new QBs are expected in Week 10, for Arizona, Baltimore, Las Vegas, Miami, and Minnesota. Three of those newbies will be making their first-ever NFL start. These QB replacements impact players at other positions. I’ll highlight that as we go. Throw in a boatload of injuries and four teams on bye, and Week 10 could be a rough one for a lot of fantasy managers. If you have a minute, check out the current wide receiver rooms for the Rams, Cardinals, and Colts. No, those aren’t made-up names you can use for phony phone calls. They’re real. Bring on Week 10! St ats of the Week Every team in the NFC North is at least three games over .500. That’s only happened in a division once, at any time, in NFL history. They all have at least six wins. 2. From the penthouse to the outhouse: All four teams in the NFC South have three wins. You can’t even make this stuff up at this point. 3. No division has ever put all four of its teams into the playoffs, but if the season ended today, all four NFC North teams would get berths in the NFC. 4. Favored teams went 14-1 in Week 9, with only the Patriots losing. 5. The Broncos have won 16 consecutive one-score games in the regular season – the longest streak all-time. 6. The QB with the longest active win streak as a starter is… J.J. McCarthy , with six consecutive wins dating back to last season. 7. Christian McCaffrey caught the 37 th touchdown pass of his career on Sunday, moving him past Marshall Faulk for most by a running back in the Super Bowl era. 8. The Raiders have given up 30+ points in six straight games, tying an NFL record. 9. Fantasy stat #1: Ashton Jeanty’s receiving line on Sunday: Five catches for negative five yards. 10. Fantasy Stat #2 : Both the Bengals and Packers have two wide receivers in the Top-8 at the position on a fantasy points per game (FPPG) basis. On to week 10. Note: NE @ DET is being played in Munich. Set those lineups early! Good news for those on the West Coast – this is the last international game of the season. Bye Weeks: Bears, Broncos, Buccaneers, Eagles Week 10 Rides, Fades and Sleepers For those who are familiar with this column, you know the drill. For everyone else: The Rides, Fades, and Sleepers is an analysis of players that I think are primed for an especially strong or poor performance, often as compared to consensus expectations. This isn’t a straight-up Start/Sit exercise. As a general rule, start your studs. I’ll rarely list the most obvious names at a position as “Rides” because those players are almost always expected to have strong performances. You don’t need me or anyone else telling you to start Jahmyr Gibbs . While this analysis is intended for season-long play, it works for DFS formats too. Half PPR scoring and Expert Consensus Rankings (ECR) are used for the column. Each week, I’m picking a Ride, Fade, and Sleeper of the Week. The rules: The Ride of the Week can’t be a truly elite option, the Fade can’t be someone who nobody is starting anyway, and the Sleeper must be an actual sleeper, from down in the rankings. Last week, my Rides, Fades, and Sleepers did well, with a lot more hits than misses, led by Fade of the Week Zay Flowers (3.8 fantasy points). You can check my work here . * * * Ride of the Week: James Cook (vs. NYJ). Maybe Cook should be listed among the elite options. He’s quietly had a great season, with a touchdown in every week but one, but he hasn’t had that monster game yet (he hasn’t topped 22 fantasy points in a week). A surprising lack of work in the passing game, and Josh Allen gobbling up rushing TDs, has held him back. Well, I think this is the week. The Bills are 8.5 point favorites, and the Jets have a generous run defense. They’ve allowed the tenth most FPPG and fifth most rushing yards to opposing backs, plus 11 total TDs. Cook should smash this week. Fade of the Week: Ashton Jeanty (@SEA). Jeanty hasn’t topped 10 carries or 27 rushing yards in his last five outings, and he hasn’t scored more than 13.5 fantasy points since his breakout in Week 1. Receiving work has kept him afloat, and I don’t know how that’s going to work in Fernando Mendoza’s debut, which couldn’t come in a worse spot than against Seattle. If the Raiders score ten points, I’ll be surprised. Their implied total is 17 and I think that’s unlikely. Jeanty is a clear sit for me this week. Sleeper of the Week: DeMario Douglas (vs. DET). Douglas has emerged as New England’s top receiver amid all the injuries, and they’re going to need plenty from him against the Lions. He quietly put up three Top-12 weekly finishes at his position in the last five weeks. Detroit’s defense has played much better of late, but that was against Miami and Minnesota. They’re still allowing the seventh most FPPG to opposing WRs. This game has the second highest Vegas total of the week (51.5). Douglas is ranked outside the Top-25 receivers this week and that’s too low – he’s a solid WR2 this week. Quarterback: Elite options this week – Josh Allen , Drake Maye, Brock Purdy, and Joe Burrow ; the analysis starts below them. Rides: Three QBs ranked in the Top-10 this week who I think will outperform: Dak Prescott (vs. SF). The 49ers defense is playing well this season (ninth fewest FPPG allowed to QBs), but that doesn’t scare me off this pick. The 49ers’ offense is elite, even with all the injuries, and the Cowboys’ “defense” isn’t likely to offer much resistance. Dallas is going to need to score to keep up, and Prescott should be slinging it. The Vegas total for this game is one of the highest of the season (55.5). Trevor Lawrence (@TEN). The risk here is that he won’t need to throw all that much – which happened last week against the impotent Ravens. I’ll take that chance. The Titans have allowed the fourth most passing yards in the NFL and they’ve also yielded three rushing TDs to opposing QBs. They also traded away their most impactful player in Jeffery Simmons. I think they’ll keep the game competitive for a while. Lawrence should do enough damage before the game is out of hand. Jared Goff (@NE) has to be licking his chops after what Jordan Love did to New England’s secondary. It was big play after big play, and Goff can do that too with his excellent receiving weapons. I’m sure the Patriots will play better, but Goff was frustrated by Miami and Minnesota the last two weeks and is due for one of his big games. Three others in the Top-12 who I like to beat their projections this week: Patrick Mahomes (@ATL), Tyler Shough (vs. CAR), and Jayden Daniels (@NYG). Daniels ran for over 100 yards and two TDs in the first meeting with New York (NOTE – bad weather could be an issue). Sleepers: Bryce Young (@NO) is always a tough call. He threw three TDs last week, and on the season he’s the QB11. But he’s been highly inconsistent, with four games with 20+ fantasy points and three with fewer than 14. I like him this week, against a mediocre (at best) New Orleans defense that’s bottom-third against QBs, and in a game that should be back-and-forth with plenty of scoring. He’s ranked outside the Top-12 QBs this week and I think he’ll have a Top-10 finish. Other QB2-types to consider if you need it: Drew Lock (@LV, who is allowing a ton of points and the third most FPPG to opposing QBs), Geno Smith (vs. BUF), J.J. McCarthy (vs. WAS, allowing the fourth most FPPG to opposing QBs, but again, watch the weather), and Jacoby Brissett (vs. LAC). Fades: Jordan Love (vs. MIN) is playing out of his mind, and I wouldn’t sit him unless you’ve got another really good QB. But Minnesota’s defense is no joke, and on Monday night they held Josh Allen to a season-low 14 fantasy points. Love leads the NFL in passing yards, so…

title: Survey results: Giants fans are confident ahead of Thursday Night Football
summary: New York Giants fans are confident in their team. We didn’t really need a poll to tell us that much. But considering Las Vegas only has the Giants as slim 1.5-point favorites (per FanDuel) over the Washington Commanders, we wanted to see just how confident Giants’ fans are heading into the rematch. Our survey question […]
full_text: New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images New York Giants fans are confident in their team. We didn’t really need a poll to tell us that much. But considering Las Vegas only has the Giants as slim 1.5-point favorites ( per FanDuel ) over the Washington Commanders, we wanted to see just how confident Giants’ fans are heading into the rematch. Our survey question this week was quick and simple: Do you think the Giants will win? While I suspect few fans are expecting a pretty game, the answer is pretty conclusive. A full 92% of Giants fans are confident in a win over the Commanders. That is, honestly, more than I was expecting. The Giants came out a bit flat against the Eagles in Week 9, and their offensive line didn’t look good at all. There’s also the ever-present concern of Jayden Daniels using his athleticism against the Giants’ aggressive man coverage based defense. The Giants have had a habit of playing sloppy and taking games down to the closing seconds. They’ve been remarkably resilient in dealing with adversity, and that’s largely been their saving grace this year. Even when they screw up, they aren’t letting those mistakes snowball. Peeking over at a similar question on our Commanders sister site, Hogs’ Haven, their fan base isn’t nearly as optimistic. Their fans are split, slightly favoring the Giants in this game 47-46%, with 7%expecting another tie. Overall, the confidence in a win over the Commanders is in line with the overall confidence of fans in their team. Like I said above, Giants fans are confident and 97% of fans believe that the team is headed in the right direction. That’s a slight bump from last week’s 96%, despite the team not able to land a difference maker ahead of the trade deadline. Or perhaps the bump has something to do with the Giants hanging onto their picks and not trading for a veteran running back or defensive tackle.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NFL predictions: Our picks for Giants-Commanders, the full Week 10 slate
summary: The New York Giants and Washington Commanders kick off Week 10 of the NFL season Thursday night at what promises to be a rainy, chilly MetLife Stadium. Can the Giants solidify their NFC East lead, or will the race for the division title tighten? Here is how the Big Blue View staff sees that game, […]
full_text: The Giants and Commanders played to a draw five weeks ago. Who wll win this time? | Getty Images The New York Giants and Washington Commanders kick off Week 10 of the NFL season Thursday night at what promises to be a rainy, chilly MetLife Stadium. Can the Giants solidify their NFC East lead, or will the race for the division title tighten? Here is how the Big Blue View staff sees that game, and the rest of the Week 10 matchups. Chris Pflum Which version of the Giants will show up on Thursday night? Will we get the sloppy Giants that came out flat against the Philadelphia Eagles, or the tough, physical, and technically sound Giants that showed up against the Houston Texans? John Harbaugh’s 9-1 record home record on Thursday Nights is encouraging. I would say that this is a game the Giants should win on paper, particularly with Washington missing some of their best players and their starting center in the concussion protocol. However, I’m also not convinced that these Giants can play a normal game and just take care of business. I keep waiting for the Giants to play a complete game and execute on offense and defense, but this team seems unable to be both consistent and explosive. I hope the offensive line comes prepared to bully an injured Washington defensive line and J.J. McCarthy isn’t forced into low percentage throws every third down by long yardage situations. Likewise, I hope that Dennard Wilson comes out swinging on defense, but also has a counterpunch ready in case Jayden Daniels has an answer to the Cover-0 blitz. I’m picking the Giants here, but they can’t afford to take Washington lightly or give Jayden Daniels the chance to catch his breath and swing the game. Pick: Giants Tony Del Genio This is the Giants’ second consecutive must-win game. You wouldn’t think that when 5-2-1 plays 2-5-1, but (1) the Giants haven’t beaten the Commanders since Jayden Daniels became their quarterback (even though Daniels didn’t play in one of those losses), (2) despite their record, Washington has beaten the Seahawks and only narrowly lost to the 49ers and Rams while the Giants were beaten soundly by the Rams, the only good team they’ve faced, and still have the 49ers and Seahawks coming up, along with the Jaguars and Lions. A division loss greatly weakens their hold on the NFC East lead, their only real path to the playoffs. Terry McLaurin is out for the season, but in his place is Stefon Diggs, who did not face the Giants in the first game. Jacory Crosky-Merritt, who beat the Giants’ run D for a 33-yard TD right off the bat in the first game, is also out. The Commanders are further decimated by injuries since their last meeting to key starters such as DT Daron Payne and IOL Lucas Patrick. So really the Giants should prevail. The problem is…containing the running of Daniels, which they did not do well in their first meeting (103 yards, by far his highest of the season, and his only 2 rushing TDs of the season). Hopefully Dennard Wilson will have a plan for that. If so, and if the Giants execute it, then the Giants can win. Pick: Giants David Hartman The rematch of the NFL’s only tie game of the season will be played in prime time on Thursday night, and for the ninth time in nine games, the Giants are playing a team that doesn’t have a winning record. But you can throw the records out the window: The 5-2-1 Giants, at home, are just 1.5 point favorites over the 2-5-1 Commanders. Go figure… Big Blue won with defense and a strong kicking game on Sunday in Philadelphia, with Arvel Reese perhaps becoming a star in real time. It was an ugly win, with the offense producing just 19 points. The Giants will need more than that against Jayden Daniels and company on Thursday night. Cam Skattebo is expected back, and that’s good news. New York couldn’t run the ball on Sunday, which stagnated their offense. Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf) might miss this game, however, and the O-line struggled at Philadelphia as it was. J.J. McCarthy wasn’t terrible on Sunday, but he wasn’t especially good either and now he’s dealing with a hip pointer. Jameis Winston led New York on its only touchdown drive while McCarthy was temporarily knocked from the game. McCarthy hasn’t thrown a TD pass (or an interception) in either of his two starts. This figures to be a close game, just like the first one. It’ll be fun to watch standout rookies Reese and Sonny Styles — college teammates at Ohio State last season — leading the way for each defense. Seriously – how did anyone score on the Buckeyes? Anyway, Dennard Wilson needs to find a way to keep Daniels from gashing his defense with his legs. He ran for 103 yards and two scores in the first game. This game could come down to intangibles like turnovers and special teams. The G-Men have been winning (or tying) close games and that’s a reflection on good coaching to a degree, and favorable luck. In a game that should be close, who am I to pick against that? Pick: Giants in a squeaker Valentine’s View We are not picking games by the spread here, but I am surprised the Giants are just 1.5-point favorites. That indicates a continuing lack of real belief in the Giants in the betting market. The Giants understand the opportunity they have in front of them, and how important this game is. In the rainy, windy, miserable conditions at MetLife Stadium Thursday evening I think you have to expect what has become a typical Giants game this season — close, somewhat sloppy, decided by who makes the plays and who properly handles the situations at the end of the game. I have far more faith in the Giants to do that than I do the Commanders. We all remember the Commanders stunning clock mismanagement at the end of the Week 5 tie with the Giants. That sort of questionable decision-making has continued to plague Washington, which is 1-3-1 in games decided by one score. If you could the Arizona game, which I do since it was decided on the game’s final play, seven of the Giants eight games this season were one-score games. The Giants are 5-1-1 in those games. They have lived on the edge, and have shown an ability to survive. Is that formula sustainable forever? Maybe not. It does, though, make me feel good about the Giants’ chances on Thursday.
