title: 49ers bold predictions review: How August takes look in November
summary: Back in August, before the season started, I dropped my four bold predictions for the 2026 San Francisco 49ers.  I am personally a fan of accountability, so while bold predictions are meant to be a little wild and out there, I wanted to go back and see just how close I was. Hold myself accountable, […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in August, before the season started, I dropped my four bold predictions for the 2026 San Francisco 49ers. I am personally a fan of accountability, so while bold predictions are meant to be a little wild and out there, I wanted to go back and see just how close I was. Hold myself accountable, you know? And while I feel good about some, others I feel less than good about. Let’s make a midseason critique of my pre-season bold predictions: The 49ers go 6-0 against the NFC West I feel so good about this that I don’t really consider this one a bold prediction anymore for two reasons: The 49ers are the best team in the division (which could have been expected before the season started) and The Rams and Seahawks aren’t great (something that wasn’t expected). The 49ers are halfway to a perfect divisional record, and the two toughest games are already out of the way. San Francisco easily disposed of the Rams in Australia in Week 1 and then pulled a close one out over the Seahawks in Seattle in Week 5. Sandwiched between those two was a one-possession win over Arizona in Week 3. Oddly enough, with Seattle and the Rams still on the schedule, the toughest battle for perfection might be the last with that Week 18 game in Arizona. If the 49ers can continue to have the grip on the NFC West they have right now, it’s possible San Francisco would have nothing to play for in this game and give the starters a rest (and maybe some gamesmanship to worsen Arizona’s draft position). Of all the preseason bold predictions, this is the one I feel best about. Mike Evans sets a career-high in receptions I still can’t believe Evans has never had 100 receptions in a season. 11 seasons in a row with at least 1,000 receiving yards, but never once triple-digit receptions. Amazing. And while Evans has clearly been the 49ers’ No. 1 receiver, this one will fall short for two reasons: His 4.5 receptions per game in his six games played would come out to 76-77 receptions over the 17-game season. Silly of me to expect a triple-digit reception season from a 49ers offense that loves to spread the ball around. The whole Achilles injury thing has me concerned about the next time we will even see Evans play. Even though he won’t set a career-high in receptions, it is easy to see the impact Evans has had on the 49ers offense. Once Evans gets back to playing shape, him playing alongside Keenan Allen could make for an even more explosive offense. Jack Jones leads the 49ers in interceptions Can’t win them all. Sometimes you have to go to Atlanta for an early game right before the bye week. But I guess we aren’t completely dead, as the 49ers brought Jones back to the practice squad on Wednesday. Shout out, Renardo Green. Maxx Crosby will be a 49er at some point I am frustrated by the 49ers’ trade deadline. I think they did a good job with who they acquired. The DeForest Buckner trade was a great move, and the Gracen Halton injury only solidified how important bringing Buckner back was. And the Allen trade shores up the receiving corps and allows the 49ers to slow-play Evans’ return from his Achilles injury. Despite it being a good deadline for the 49ers, it’s borderline criminal they didn’t add another defensive end. Step into my world of insanity because I recognize it takes two to tango to make a trade, and it was unlikely Crosby would be dealt at the deadline, but it would be so nice for the 49ers to maybe overpay with picks one time to make a big move. The two biggest trades of the Shanahan/Lynch era have been Trent Williams and Christian McCaffrey, and the 49ers only had to give up two thirds, a fourth, and two fifths to get the two franchise cornerstones. The only time the 49ers took a big swing trading multiple first-round picks was the infamous move up to pick No. 3 to take Trey Lance. And sure, maybe the 49ers are a little shy to make that type of move after the poor results last time, but Maxx Crosby isn’t a project quarterback; he’s a proven entity. It couldn’t have hurt the 49ers to offer the same two first-round picks that originally got Crosby sent to the Ravens and maybe tack on an additional day-two pick to sweeten the deal and force the Raiders to say no. Would anybody miss the picks if Crosby is what pushes the 49ers over the top for a Lombardi Trophy? I doubt it. But let’s snap back to reality: Crosby wasn’t going to happen, the Chargers apparently think 0-8 is an easy hole to climb out of and wouldn’t move off of Khalil Mack, and the Texans had no reason to trade Jadeveon Clowney. But somebody like Will McDonald felt like he could have been had. He requested a trade, and the Jets have enough depth on the end where McDonald could be expended. One would assume if the 49ers called, they were looking for value over getting the player as they do, but why not slightly overpay to ensure you get the guy? The 49ers are at the position where they can. Let’s say the 49ers valued McDonald with the fifth-round pick they hold for the 2027 draft. Why not overpay and offer a third instead (knowing comp picks will be coming) to get the asset that will help a position right now? But again, it takes two to make a deal. The 49ers had a successful trade deadline with Buckner and Allen; it just feels like some meat was left on the bone by not making a move for a defensive end.
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: 3 things to watch in 49ers-Cowboys: Run the football, Kyle
summary: The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys will meet on Sunday and continue a storied history between the two franchises. What was once a rivalry has turned into an avalanche, with the 49ers’ winning streak over the Cowboys spanning several years. Sunday is expected to be a high-scoring affair with two high-powered offenses, and Vegas […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys will meet on Sunday and continue a storied history between the two franchises. What was once a rivalry has turned into an avalanche, with the 49ers’ winning streak over the Cowboys spanning several years. Sunday is expected to be a high-scoring affair with two high-powered offenses, and Vegas believes it too, with the highest implied total of the weekend. Former pass game coordinator and defensive backs coach for the Philadelphia Eagles under Vic Fangio, Christian Parker took over as defensive coordinator for Dallas this season, and let’s just say things have not gone well. Kyle Shanahan and the 49ers know starting linebacker Dee Winters very well also. You can bet Shanahan and Brock Purdy will have the Cowboys’ linebackers in a bind constantly on Sunday. What else will the 49ers look to exploit on Sunday? Here are three things to watch for Sunday. The 49ers’ rushing attack It may not feel like it, but the 49ers’ rushing attack is number one in several reliable metrics. Not only are the 49ers number one in EPA/play (0.14), success rate (52.1%), and total EPA (66.26; Buffalo is second at 53.09), but they also lead in EPA/ rush, with Buffalo at 0.05 and a league-high success rate on the ground of 50.4%. Dallas’ defense ranks 27th in the NFL with an EPA/rush allowed of -0.02 and 25th in success rate allowed on the ground at 43.2%. After facing the worst run defense in the league in total rushing yards allowed last week, the 49ers face the second-worst run defense in Dallas with 1,327 rushing yards allowed and 4.99 rushing yards per attempt. Even pushing to a heavier box count is unlikely, as Dallas has an 18.1% rate. That number is good for 30th in the NFL. That 40-carry number is in the 49ers’ sights for a second consecutive week. 49ers motion percentage The 49ers hold a slight edge in motion percentage over the Miami Dolphins at 73.% to Miami’s 73.2% for the league high mark. It’s not just the amount of motion, but the types of motions, which include the often-used banana motions from Kyle Juszczyk. The advantages of the motion in the run game, to change number counts, and in the pass game to help identify coverages are a huge part of the offense. Dallas is dead last with a 0.11 EPA allowed per play against motion. Good luck, Dallas. The 49ers rank fourth in motion at snap with 50.6%. Dak Prescott against the 49ers’ preferred coverages The 49ers are primarily a zone coverage defense, specifically Cover 3. Under Raheem Morris, the 49ers haven’t changed their defensive coverage base much, but there has been an increase in man coverage looks, even if the increase isn’t significant in comparison to zone looks. Dak Prescott has punished Cover 3 with his third-highest EPA per play of 0.231. On 79 attempts, Prescott averages 7.9 YPA. Against Cover 0, which is a blitz coverage, Prescott struggled mightily with an EPA of -0.276, but he has only 29 attempts. The 49ers failed to pressure Michael Penix in Atlanta, and a similar output won’t go over well against Dallas and their offense. Nick Bosa and DeForest Buckner must turn up the heat Sunday. Perhaps an Osa Odighizuwa revenge game?

Shanahan said Allen’s head was “probably spinning” Wednesday. Allen didn’t disagree. He has played for Colts, Bears and Chargers during his 179-game career, but has never been part of a Shanahan-influenced offense. Allen explained that the concepts were familiar, but the verbiage was a foreign language. “I’m just going to have to kind of flip everything in the brain,” Allen said, “and learn a new terminology.” How hard might that be? Offered Samuel: “I ain’t going to lie, this s— is tough.” “My rookie year, I’d say it probably took me about eight nine weeks to really be comfortable in the offense,” Samuel said. “But, honestly, some people are picking it up faster than others, so we’ll just see how it goes.” 49ers injury updates: Nate Hobbs returns to practice “Cornerback Nate Hobbs is a full go. With both starting cornerbacks out, and the only other option being rookie Ephesians Prysock, the Niners may give the veteran an opportunity. Lenoir and Green not practicing also explains why the 49ers added Jack Jones to the practice squad. Last week, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said Hobbs has the versatility to play inside or outside. Shanahan said, “Nate’s a real good NFL corner. Seen him at a number of places. We’ve scrimmaged against him. I’ve played against him in games. He didn’t have a long camp, but he had long enough with us that you could see him effective inside, effective outside. His versatility is great. Where he’s needed.” Backup QB Mac Jones happy to remain with 49ers after trade deadline uncertainty “What’s the price tag on that?” Jones asked. “To me, it’s multiple millions of dollars to have fun and be on a winning team because I’ve been on the other side of that, too, when you’re not really having fun and you’re not winning.” CJ West, Deebo Samuel to return to 49ers practice; Mike Evans remains out “The 49ers on Wednesday re-signed veteran cornerback Jack Jones to the practice squad. Jones appeared in the first seven games of the season and was released after he struggled in the 49ers’ 29-20 loss to the Atlanta Falcons on Oct. 25.”

title: Should the Titans re-sign Tony Pollard after declining to trade him?
summary: The Tennessee Titans were very active leading up to the NFL trade deadline. They traded Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, and Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills. By doing so, Mike Borgonzi acquired four total picks, including two first-rounders for Simmons, and an additional second-rounder for Hooker. One player who was not traded was […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 27: Tony Pollard #20 of the Tennessee Titans is tackled after carrying the ball against the New York Giants during the first quarter at MetLife Stadium on September 27, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans were very active leading up to the NFL trade deadline . They traded Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, and Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills . By doing so, Mike Borgonzi acquired four total picks, including two first-rounders for Simmons, and an additional second-rounder for Hooker. One player who was not traded was running back Tony Pollard. Reports had consistently indicated the Titans preferred to hold onto Pollard because he’s been helping with the development and evaluation of Cam Ward. Regardless of how that makes you feel, it seems those reports were accurate. Pollard is in a contract year. It was previous GM Ran Carthon who signed the former Memphis standout to a three-year, $21.7 million contract prior to the 2024 campaign. Pollard is currently the 22nd-highest paid back in the league, proving that contract has aged well. But declining opportunities to trade a 29-year-old RB on an expiring contract when you’re rebuilding the roster is an interesting tactic. It makes us wonder if Borgonzi is considering re-signing Pollard. He’s due for unrestricted free agency. The running back market has been reset by recent deals for Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs, and Saquon Barkley. They are among four RBs earning more than $20 million annually (alongside Jonathan Taylor). Pollard obviously isn’t that tier of back, but the increases in pay will impact his negotiations, too. Given Pollard’s age, the Titans shouldn’t re-sign him to longer than a two-year extension. Given his advancing age, they’ll want to protect themselves against overpaying for a declining talent. Signing Pollard to a two-year, $20 million contract feels fair. Pollard would earn $10 million annually, making him the 16th-highest paid back in the NFL right behind Kyren Williams ($11m AAV). Other happenings around the league might impact this, but that feels like the appropriate range for a Pollard extension.

title: How Commanders’ Jayden Daniels responded after two late picks vs. Giants
summary: Jayden Daniels had 207 consecutive pass attempts without tossing an interception. Then he had two picks in four throws late in the fourth quarter of Thursday night’s must-win game against the Giants.  In two words, not great.  The second interception came with 2 minutes, 15 seconds left and Washington down four. Dan Quinn had three […]
full_text: Jayden Daniels had 207 consecutive pass attempts without tossing an interception . Then he had two picks in four throws late in the fourth quarter of Thursday night’s must-win game against the Giants. In two words, not great. The second interception came with 2 minutes, 15 seconds left and Washington down four. Dan Quinn had three timeouts and the two-minute warning, but there was no guarantee Daniels would see the ball again. He eventually would, and earned Washington a crucial 24-21 victory . At the time, Daniels understood his interceptions might’ve cost his team the game. The third-year pro chose not to dwell on that. There would be plenty of time for critique on the plane, back at the facility and over the weekend watching film. This was not that time. Daniels shut out negative thoughts and remained locked in. “It won’t do anything for me to still dwell on (the mistakes),” Daniels said in his postgame press conference . “Everybody on the sideline (said) the defense is gonna give you the opportunity to go out there and win the game.” Sonny Styles provided that. The rookie linebacker sniffed out a designed J.J. McCarthy run on third down and pounced, with a tackle for loss that forced a punt. Sonny Styles said absolutely not on 3rd down. WASvsNYG on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/1d9S7zwsT3 — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 Daniels had one more shot. That fact didn’t weigh him down one bit. Nor did the importance of getting this win. “I think you understand the magnitude of the moment, and you’re not really thinking about the season,” Daniels said. “In that moment, you’re really thinking about winning this game, and that’s kind of just the biggest thing for me. I didn’t want to let my team down in that moment, so when they gave me another opportunity to go out there and win the game, I didn’t want to let them down.” He took it without hesitation and despite previous mistakes, connected with Stefon Diggs on a 31-yard touchdown catch-and-run with less than a minute left. He took a deep shot on the first play, where Treylon Burks earned a pass interference call. Then came a one-yard scramble and a short completion to Austin Ekeler. On the next play, Daniels saw something he could exploit with Stefon Diggs in the right slot. “Cover zero,” Daniels said. “They’re going to heat us up in those moments. I gave a little signal to Stef, and he went on the slant, and the rest is history.” HE'S LIKE THAT 📺 #WASvsNYG @nflonprime pic.twitter.com/0uyAKgkMeD — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 13, 2026 It took a Rasul Douglas interception to officially seal it, but Daniels’ resilience after two disappointments was crucial to the Commanders winning this game. If he caves, the Commanders lose. Daniels got it done and earned the sixth comeback in the fourth quarter or overtime in his young NFL career. This one might’ve been trying, but Daniels didn’t let it show. “Baby Kobe,” Diggs said. “He ain’t flinch. He’s going to be the same kind of player at the beginning of the game and at the end of the game. For me, things are going to happen, good and bad. He isn’t going to change. I had 100% faith.” What did you think of Jayden Daniels coming through after two costly interceptions? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Commanders report card: Team grades in NFL Week 10 win vs. Giants
summary: The Commanders certainly needed that.  Washington got a massive 24-21 victory over the New York Giants on Thursday night that essentially saved their season, keeping the Commanders in the NFC East race. A loss would’ve been devastating.  That win at MetLife Stadium gives them a glimmer of hope. What they do with it remains to […]
full_text: The Commanders certainly needed that. Washington got a massive 24-21 victory over the New York Giants on Thursday night that essentially saved their season, keeping the Commanders in the NFC East race. A loss would’ve been devastating. That win at MetLife Stadium gives them a glimmer of hope. What they do with it remains to be seen, but this game brought some positivity back to Washington after finally coming through in the clutch. This one was all about resilience and character in an imperfect game with several big mistakes, but the Commanders never stopped pushing. Not after Jayden Daniels threw two fourth-quarter interceptions. Not after the defense gave up an explosive touchdown to Isaiah Likely. Jayden Daniels kept throwing. Daronte Jones kept sending pressure. This was the four-quarter game Dan Quinn has been questing for. It was imperfect to say the least, but Washington seemed to understand the moment and never, ever stopped swinging. To see that type of fight in this massive moment, after all the adversity faced, was impressive. Let’s take a deeper dive into the Commanders performance in this Week 10 report card: Rushing offense I was fairly critical of the Commanders running game in the takeaways article . I don’t take that back. This running game is not revving at the right RPM, with blocking issues preventing efficiency in the operation. The Commanders averaged 3.2 yards per carry, and that included an explosive Rachaad White run that makes his stats look better than they otherwise would have. Even Jayden Daniels wasn’t getting loose on scrambles – the Giants seemed committed to keeping him in the pocket – or getting loose on designed runs that have been increasingly rare this season. However, offensive coordinator David Blough’s commitment to the run game was impressive, with 33 carries equal to the number of pass attempts in the game. That helped the play action passing game and kept the Giants defense honest, which was smart. If Washington can get the running game up to 4ish yards per carry in this season, they’ll be feeling good. That didn’t happen on this night. Grade: D Passing offense Jayden Daniels hadn’t thrown an interception all season. Then he threw two of them in four pass attempts. Late in the fourth quarter. With the game on the line. The Commanders got the ball back and Jayden made the most of it with a dagger 31-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs with a minute left to take a lead that they never surrendered. Daniels completed 23-of-33 passes for 249 yards, and those two picks, for a 96.7 rating. A previously-beleaguered offensive line was good in pass protection. Like, really good. Pressures allowed from the Commanders OL tonight (41 pass pro snaps each): • Brandon Coleman: 1 • Chris Paul: 0 • Nick Allegretti: 0 • Sam Cosmi: 0 • Josh Conerly Jr: 3 For Cosmi and Paul, they’ve allowed just two sacks combined in 677 pass pro snaps so far in 2026. — Ryan Fowler (@_RyanFowler_) November 13, 2026 Washington got vital contributions from Stefon Diggs and tight end Ben Sinnott. Diggs led the team with six catches for 83 yards and that huge victory-sealing score. Sinnott had four catches for 42 yards and a touchdown despite having just one previous catch all season. The protection factor can’t be ignored. Neither can the two picks. The passing game needed some defensive help, but it came through at the end of the half, and, most importantly, at the end of the game. Grade: B-plus Rushing defense Cam Skattebo is a crazy person, in a super fun way. He was motivated in this one, and had 78 yards and two touchdowns on 18 carries. J.J. McCarthy averaged 5.7 yards per carry and had some big runs. That’s not ideal. Neither was the 4.3 yards per carry that Washington’s defense allowed. Then there was that had-to-have it third-and-1 in the fourth quarter, when Deatrich Wise and the crew shut a quarterback sneak down when the Commanders had to have it. The same is true of Sonny Styles tackling McCarthy for a loss on a key third down late in the game. That’s worth something, too. Grade: B-minus Passing defense The pass rush was active as heck. Maybe not with a four-man rush, but the blitz was largely effective, especially with Nick Cross and Jeremy Reaves coming in from the defensive backfield. Sonny Styles and Frankie Luvu came a ton, too. Frankie Luvu got a huge forced fumble that produced a takeaway. The nine catches and 127 yards to tight end Isaiah Likely weren’t great. The Commanders handled Malik Nabers relatively well. Rasul Douglas called game with that fourth-quarter interception. Washington brought it, and stood tall when it mattered most. The Commanders had just one sack, but hit McCarthy six times and forced errant throws. They were relentless in pursuit of the quarterback. Grade: A-minus Special teams It won’t show up in the stat sheet, but Luke McCaffrey’s heads-up play to give Washington the ball at the 40 was such a baller move, a sky-high football IQ play that was crucial to a late-game effort. Drew Stevens made a field goal and vital extra points. Tress Way had a 49.0-yard net punt average and Kain Medrano nearly ended the game with a ball punched free on that last Giants kick return. Washington just didn’t recover it. Grade: A-minus Coaching We’ve passed out lots of Fs in this category. Not tonight. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones gets a game ball after sending relentless pressure even after his defense allowed some explosives. The game plan was sound and so were the play calls. David Blough wasn’t quite as strong – going to the well with the same pass play one too many times led to Daniels’ second pick – but the Commanders got the job done. Also, Dan Quinn gets some kudos. His challenge on third-and-short was vital. He managed to keep his team together despite great adversity, and got them to perform well under pressure. The Commanders had to win this one, and they did. Quinn deserves credit for that. Jones deserves a game ball. Grade: A How would you grade each phase of the Commanders’ game in a huge win over the Giants? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Key takeaways from Washington Commanders win vs. Giants in NFL Week 10
summary: The Commanders minced no words when discussing the importance of Thursday night’s game against the New York Giants.  It was a must-win for Washington. Jayden Daniels said it. K’Lavon Chaisson, too. Dan Quinn avoided the phrase but emphasized Thursday’s importance time and again.  While that sounds like a reach with nearly half Washington’s season left […]
full_text: The Commanders minced no words when discussing the importance of Thursday night’s game against the New York Giants. It was a must-win for Washington. Jayden Daniels said it. K’Lavon Chaisson, too. Dan Quinn avoided the phrase but emphasized Thursday’s importance time and again. While that sounds like a reach with nearly half Washington’s season left to play, it’s shockingly fair. The win put the Commanders in the mix and within striking distance of the Giants, who lead a weak NFC East by a little bit. A loss would have put Washington four back with eight to play, a virtually insurmountable lead to block a path to the postseason. The Commanders lit their margin of error on fire in the early going of the regular season, with one blown opportunity after another. Washington simply had to win this one. The Commanders were able to do that in stunning fashion. The Daronte Jones defense came up huge in the fourth quarter, and the Commanders finally surged ahead to secure a 24-21 victory over the Giants at MetLife Stadium. Let’s take a look at what we learned about the Commanders while watching this Thursday night contest live: Commanders (finally) come through The Commanders had found themselves with a fourth-quarter lead or tie for their third straight Thursday night game. Washington’s 4th quarter lead over the Giants evaporated with a disastrous 66-yard catch-and-run on a pass from J.J. McCarthy to tight end Isaiah Likely with roughly eight minutes left. The Commanders found themselves, as they have so many times before, needing clutch performances to close out the game. They had previously failed so regularly in those moments that it set up this do-or-die Week 10 scenario that had been discussed all week. How would they respond with so much on the line? As it happens, they responded poorly to start, with Jayden Daniels’ first interception of the season. The Commanders were moving the ball well when Daniels – often accused of playing it too safe – took a deep shot to Chig Okonkwo. The ball was too far inside and allowed Giants safety Jevon Holland to make a play on the ball. JEVÓN WAS READY FOR IT 🔒 📺: PRIME VIDEO pic.twitter.com/rcpn8j7ak6 — New York Giants (@Giants) November 13, 2026 He picked it off with roughly five minutes left. But the Commanders wouldn’t let that be Daniels’ final pass of the night; the defense came up huge on a third-and-1 – a Jameis Winston sneak was ruled a first-down but then overturned on a Dan Quinn challenge – and the Commanders got the ball back. What would they do with this second chance? As it turned out, Daniels threw another pick on fourth-and-1, operating from shotgun and with an unreal call for the situation. Here’s a look at it: ANOTHER INTERCEPTION FOR THE GIANTS. WASvsNYG on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/slrEYfPyCj — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 The Commanders still had three timeouts and the two-minute warning to get the ball back. They did that, somehow. So, let’s ask this question again: What would they do with this (third) chance? Well, Stefon Diggs came up huge. The veteran receiver got open quickly and Daniels found him for a 32-yard, go-ahead touchdown. HE'S LIKE THAT 📺 #WASvsNYG @nflonprime pic.twitter.com/0uyAKgkMeD — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 13, 2026 Young pass catchers step up The Commanders entered Thursday’s game with Terry McLaurin on injured reserve, expecting tight end Chig Okonkwo to pair with Stefon Diggs to pace the passing game. But Okonkwo left this game and headed into the locker room early and was questionable to return with a back injury. Uh, oh. That meant Daniels had to find new targets. The quarterback did exactly that. He got Ben Sinnott heavily involved, despite the young tight end entering the night with just one catch. He had some beauties in this game, including a catch-and-acrobatic-leap over a would-be tackler. . @ben_sinnott hurdle 😌 pic.twitter.com/2vZscUVTyi — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 13, 2026 Then he scored a key touchdown at the end of the half. COME ONNNNN 82 📺 #WASvsNYG @nflonprime pic.twitter.com/f6A9zDZeb2 — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 13, 2026 After intermission, on a gut-check drive after allowing New York to steal the lead early in the second half, Daniels found rookie Antonio Williams the ball – it was his first target of the game!! – with room to catch and run for a huge 31-yard touchdown. things we love to see: 📺 #WASvsNYG @nflonprime pic.twitter.com/IaFRzmM1jn — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) November 13, 2026 Okonkwo eventually returned in the fourth quarter, but those plays made while he was out were crucial to the Commanders staying in it deep in this game, where they need big contributions from role players. Commanders continue running aground The Commanders want to run the football. Like, really, really bad. You can tell in the commitment to the ground game, with a nearly even run-pass split in the first half of Thursday’s game despite the fact Washington averaged just 2.4 yards per carry prior to halftime. The Commanders haven’t been a good running team most of the season. Bill Croskey-Merritt, their best and most physical back, has been on injured reserve for three games. While Rachaad White can move it on the ground, the blocking has been lacking in a big way outside of right guard Sam Cosmi. That has an impact on most everything Washington does, from staying on schedule to controlling the clock. It’s no shock that the best Commanders performances have occurred when the ground game (not including Jayden Daniels’ scrambles) has gotten going. Still, they produced 60 yards or less in two of the last three games, and desperately needed better in this essential contest at New York. The Commanders were averaging 2.4 yards per carry entering the fourth quarter. The split stayed relatively even, so offensive coordinator David Blough could maintain the playaction passing threat, with play fakes providing some offensive production. Then, White had an explosive run late and Austin Ekeler had a tough fourth-quarter run. Even so, this running game is nowhere near where it should be at this point in the season. It’s hard to imagine Croskey-Merritt as a savior if he returns, as expected , next week, and the offensive line is what it is talent-wise, but Washington has got to find solutions to beef up production on the ground.

title: Commanders fan confidence sits at 14%; give us your take on why
summary: It already feels like a long season When you look back across the first half of the Commanders’ 2026 campaign, it feels as if it’s been emotionally draining. Between sudden quarterback departures, gritty backup heroics, an overseas stumble, and the occasional divisional triumph, the burgundy & gold faithful have been put through the wringer without […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 11: Head coach Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders looks on against the New York Giants during the second half of the NFL game at Northwest Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images It already feels like a long season When you look back across the first half of the Commanders’ 2026 campaign, it feels as if it’s been emotionally draining. Between sudden quarterback departures, gritty backup heroics, an overseas stumble, and the occasional divisional triumph, the burgundy & gold faithful have been put through the wringer without much positive to show for it. Every week has brought a brand new narrative, and our weekly polling numbers have mirrored every sharp spike and sudden drop. This week, we here at SB Nation & Hogs Haven are trying to do something just a little different with Reacts . Using AI, we have rendered a chart of our weekly confidence poll results dating back to the start of the season, shown as a single timeline graphic, and we have added reminders of key contextual moments along the way that helped drive the peaks and valleys. ( Note: This graphic was created using AI) Take a gander at that chart. It tells a vivid story of hopes and harsh adversity: Preseason to Week 1: Riding high at 70% entering the year, optimism crested at a season-high 83% Week 2: The bottom fell out. Jayden Daniels dislocated his elbow during a 37-20 loss to Dallas, sending fan confidence tumbling down to 20%. Week 3: Marcus Mariota stepped in off the bench to orchestrate an encouraging 33-31 home upset over the defending champion Seahawks, pushing confidence back up to 76%. Week 4: The injury bug struck again in London. Mariota went down with a knee injury, pressing rookie Athan Kaliakmanis into emergency duty in a 30-13 loss to the Colts, sending confidence back under 30%. Weeks 5 through 7: A bruising stretch, highlighted by a hard-fought tie with New York and a tough road loss in San Francisco, kept confidence pinned down around 20%. Week 8: A dominant 27-10 dismantling of the Philadelphia Eagles snapped the four-game winless drought, bumping sentiment back up to 43%. Which brings us directly to this week’s survey results. Confidence In our first question in this week’s Hogs Haven survey , we asked our standard weekly question: Are you confident in the direction of the team? Yes: 14% No: 86% That 14% mark establishes a new low for 2026, dropping well below the 40.1% season average. Let’s hear what you think Normally, this is the spot in the Reacts results article where I lay out my own detailed analysis of why the numbers moved the way they did. This week, however, I want to turn the keys over to you. Looking at the AI graphic above and reflecting on where this team sits today, what specific factors do you think are driving these numbers? Is this 14% reading simply a visceral, delayed hangover from the (extremely) bumpy first half? Are folks exhausted by the lingering quarterback shuffle, offensive inconsistency and doubts about the coaching? Or is it a pragmatic assessment of the daunting hill Washington faces in the standings? Whether your thoughts apply specifically to this week’s dip or take in the entire arc of the season to-date, I invite you to jump into the comments section below and share your analysis. The critical need for a win tonight Which leads us directly to the results from our second question of the week that looks at tonight’s high-stakes rematch: Who will win the Thursday Night Football matchup between the Commanders and the New York Giants? Visit our partners at FanDuel That split illustrates just how tight fans expect this divisional dogfight to be — but let’s be clear about the stakes: Washington must win tonight to keep its 2026 season alive. By the way, in a similar poll over at Big Blue View, the results were pretty stark: Let’s dispense with any illusions about wild card scenarios. Given the crowded NFC wild card pack, climbing that mountain from where Washington currently sits is, practically if not mathematically, out of the question. The only realistic path to playing postseason football in January is capturing the NFC East crown. Consider the mathematical difference that depends on the outcome at MetLife Stadium tonight: If the Commanders beat John Harbaugh’s Giants , Washington walks off the field with a 3-5-1 record, sitting just two games back of New York (5-3-1). More importantly, having tied New York in Week 5, a victory tonight hands Washington the head-to-head tiebreaker. With eight games left on the schedule, that two-game gap with a tiebreaker in hand represents a difficult, but potentially viable path to the division title. The Cowboys are 4.5-point home underdogs to the 49ers this week while the Eagles are on a bye. A Commanders win tonight, combined with a Cowboys loss on Sunday, could set the stage for an NFC East that would look like this: Washington would be a half-game behind the Cowboys, with a Week 18 game in Landover still on the schedule, while the Commanders would have to make up 2 games on the Giants, who still have Jacksonville, San Francisco, Seattle, Cleveland, Detroit and Dallas on their schedule, creating plenty of losing opportunities for Big Blue. If Washington loses tonight, however , the math turns catastrophic. The Commanders would fall to 2-6-1, sitting four games back of the Giants in the win column. Because New York would hold the head-to-head tiebreaker, Washington would face a functional five-game deficit with only eight games remaining. At that point, any discussion of the playoffs ceases, and the remainder of the 2026 schedule becomes a meaningless developmental epilogue. So, it all comes down to sixty minutes of football in northern New Jersey tonight. I’m an outlier here: Some of the reasons for my personal confidence While the community’s overall confidence has hit a cold snap, I’m personally not quite ready to pack it in or surrender to despair. If you look past the immediate win-loss tally, there is evidence, in my view, that units across this roster are making steady forward progress that will begin to show results in the win column even as the Cowboys struggle and the Giants face the stiffer part of their schedule against teams that the Commanders have already played. Offensively, over the full season, Washington has protected the football remarkably well, keeping the Commanders near the very top of the league in turnover differential at +8. Meanwhile, David Blough’s offensive scheme has produced a steady rate of explosive plays of 20+ yards, giving the team punch even through stretches of third-down frustration. And, while Jayden hasn’t quite looked himself in many key spots this season, I know that the ice-cold assassin is still there, and that he will emerge at some point to win the games that the Commanders haven’t been winning so far this season. 5 minutes of #Commanders QB Jayden Daniels giving the Giants problems. JD5 vs. the Giants, career: 4 starts | 0 losses | 1,117 total YDS | 5 total TD 74/106 | 69.8 CMP% | 867 YDS | 3 TD | 0 INT | 103.8 RTG 38 CAR | 250 YDS | 6.6 YPC | 2 TD 🎥: @NFL , @Commanders | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/NnFpfXNLb9 — Johnathan (@DCuratedSports) November 12, 2026 Defensively, Daronte Jones’ group has shown noticeable growth over the past few weeks. With veteran coach Steve Wilks working closely with the secondary, blown coverages have decreased significantly and communication on backend switches has sped up. Young defensive building blocks like Trey Amos and Sonny Styles are showing the sideline-to-sideline range needed to erase chunk gains in space with improved ball awareness and tackling. The self-inflicted procedural penalties and pre-snap miscues that haunted September are still there, but they seem to be tapering off, and they remain correctable. If Washington executes cleanly, this roster can be competitive against anyone remaining on the schedule —…

title: Five Washington Commanders players key to beating Giants in NFL Week 10
summary: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels didn’t mince words when discussing the importance of Thursday night’s clash with the New York Giants.   “Yeah,” Daniels said. “I think next week is a must-win.”  Daniels said that right after Sunday’s loss to the L.A. Rams, yet another one-score game that got away.   The Commanders have been backed into a […]
full_text: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels didn’t mince words when discussing the importance of Thursday night’s clash with the New York Giants. “Yeah,” Daniels said. “I think next week is a must-win.” Daniels said that right after Sunday’s loss to the L.A. Rams, yet another one-score game that got away. The Commanders have been backed into a corner, with essentially no margin for error after finishing the season’s first half (essentially) at 2-5-1 despite several opportunities for better. The NFC East is in the dumps and currently paced by the Giants, who have five wins to their credit despite using three quarterbacks to this point. The Commanders must close the gap and find a way to win on Thursday night. If they don’t, their season is essentially over. That’s why Daniels called this a must-win despite the fact it’s just Week 10. This is a big one. There’s no arguing that. So Washington will need their best performance of the season, with key contributions being mandatory from these five players (not named Jayden Daniels). Let’s examine which guys must step up, and why, heading into the biggest game of the year: TE Chig Okonkwo Washington’s TE1 is starting to heat up, with an increased target share and production in recent weeks. Chig Okonkwo is a dynamic threat in the middle of the field and someone who gains tough yards after contact. Considering injuries at receiver, it’s easily argued that he’s the No. 2 receiver regardless of what his position says. He had four catches for 60 yards on six targets last time these teams met, and he needs to have another big day as a man-coverage beater. Chig is a matchup problem, and designing plays to get him the ball early could lead to a huge day. C Nick Allegretti Center Lucas Patrick, who has been starting in recent weeks, was ruled out of this game because he’s in the concussion protocol. The Commanders will not replace him with Matt Gulbin, who filled in Sunday after Patrick got hurt. Instead, they’ll go back to their original starting center , Nick Allegretti, who lost his job and moved to guard after a summer filled with injury setbacks and underperformance. Now they’ll need him to captain the line, make the right calls and checks, and help the run game succeed working on the interior, where it has struggled in recent weeks. No pressure, Nick. That’s a tough assignment heading into a massive game, but it’s as vital as any on an offense that has struggled to find consistency in run production and pass protection. CB Trey Amos It’s no surprise that the Commanders secondary is better with Trey Amos and safety Nick Cross in it. Those are two massive upgrades in terms of talent and consistency. This will mark Amos’s fourth game back . While he’s always better than the alternative, he wasn’t quite as good in a loss to the Rams. Washington needs the best version of Amos in this Giants game. Malik Nabers went off in the previous meeting, to the tune of 11 receptions for 121 yards and a touchdown on 20 targets. That was part of a four-game run exceeding 100 yards . Amos didn’t play against the Giants when they met in Landover, and Washington doesn’t shadow receivers, but the Amos/Nabers matchup will be one to watch whenever they’re lined up across each other. LB Frankie Luvu The veteran always plays with his hair on fire, but his aggressiveness has turned into steady production on the interior. He had 15 combined tackles, a sack and two quarterback hits against the Rams. Luvu has improved as a blitzer in this system and formed a solid partnership with Sonny Styles in the middle. They’ll be key to slowing the Giants’ running game, and are physical enough to handle Cam Skattebo’s aggressive style. EDGE K’Lavon Chaisson The Commanders need better from their four-man rush, and that should start with their best pass rusher. K’Lavon Chaisson was passionate about Washington’s need to improve quickly and win tonight’s game. He must lead with his play on Thursday night and make the types of game-changing plays he’s capable of while helping Washington’s defense continue trending in the right direction. title: Stats and Snaps Lite – 2026 Week 9: Rams vs. Commanders
summary: Throughout this season, the Commanders have shown a maddening inability to maintain a level of play through two halves of football.  Last week, against the Eagles, the offense struggled for most of the first half, then came alive before halftime and pulled away in the second half.  This week was almost the opposite. The Commanders […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 08: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders is sacked against the Los Angeles Rams during the fourth quarter at Northwest Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Throughout this season, the Commanders have shown a maddening inability to maintain a level of play through two halves of football. Last week, against the Eagles, the offense struggled for most of the first half, then came alive before halftime and pulled away in the second half. This week was almost the opposite. The Commanders built a 7-point lead through the first half, and then allowed the Rams’ offense to pull ahead in the second half, while failing to keep pace when they had the ball. The loss to the Rams drops the Commanders’ record to 2-5-1. Yet, surprisingly, their hopes of making the playoffs are far from extinguished, thanks to playing in the second-weakest division in football. With the NFC East and South featuring 7 teams with losing records, and the East led by the paper tiger Giants, there is a good chance that at least one team with a losing record will make the playoffs this season. And it’s still too early to rule out the possibility that 2026 will be the first season with two losing teams making the playoffs. Could Washington be one of the lucky losers? Thursday nights rematch with the Giants will be their best opportunity, and one of their last remaining chances to start making their case. Despite what the record says, the Commanders have shown the ability to play close with, and in one case, even beat good teams. But they have also found ways to lose to bad teams. So, I wouldn’t want to bet real money on the outcome. The short week ahead of the Thursday night game didn’t allow me to do my usual thorough job with the Stats & Snaps. So, this edition of the Stats & Snaps is a lite version, just emphasizing the key stats from the major contributors. There were a fair few so-so and worse performances in the 13-20 home loss to the L.A. Rams. But even in the doldrums of the Commanders’ fifth loss in 8 games, there were a few bright sparks. Were they enough for the team to catch fire down the stretch? Or were they the embers to feed the cleansing fire of another offseason recalibration? We might start to get a better idea after Thursday Night Football. While we wait to see what primetime brings, let’s have a look at who stepped up, who dropped the ball, and where everyone lined up in the disappointing loss to the visiting Rams in Northwest Stadium. OFFENSE Jayden Daniels completed 24/35 passes (68.6%, ADOT 7.7 yds) for 274 yds and 1 TD. He added 4 rushing attempts for 16 yds, with 1 fumble, forced by Myles Garrett. The fumble resulted in JD5’s first turnover of the season. His 50% rushing success rate was the highest on the team. Jayden committed a costly delay of game infraction with 8:42 remaining in the 4 th quarter. His effort was good for a 55.7 QBR, and ranked 11 th among starting QBs in Week 9. Rachaad White led the Commanders’ rushing attack with just 28 yds on 7 attempts (4 Y/A) and 0 first downs (28.6% success rate). Rachaad also caught 2/3 targets for 41 yds, with a team-leading long reception of 45 yds, most of which was gained after the catch. As a result, White had elite level receiving productivity at 3.15 Y/RR. White also had 2 fumbles and 1 recovery. The first was recovered by Washington. On the final play of the game, he recovered a fumble by Chig Okonkwo and then fumbled the ball for a turnover with time expiring. Austin Ekeler had 8 rushing attempts for 16 yds, with a long of 7 (25% success rate). He caught 2/3 targets for 18 yds, with a long of 12. Van Jefferson was the only WR listed as a starter. He led the WR group, catching 5/7 targets (71.4%), at a team-high ADOT of 12.6 yds, for 58 yds and 1 TD. That included 2 receptions out of 3 contested targets. After Rachaad White, Jefferson was by far the most productive receiver on the team at a very good 2.32 Y/RR. Stefon Diggs played primarily in the slot. He caught 3/5 targets for 51 yds, with a long of 42. He was the Commanders’ third-most productive WR at a respectable 1.76 Y/RR, and generated an impressive 8.0 YAC/rec. Despite getting the lion’s share of playing time, Antonio Williams only caught 3/6 targets for 25 yds, with 1 drop, at an ADOT of 9.8 yds. He was the Commanders’ least productive receiver at an anemic 0.68 Y/RR. Jayden Bradley took advantage of his elevation from the practice squad to record his first NFL reception for 12 yds. Luke McCaffery got on the field for 9 offensive plays and caught 1 pass for 6 yds. Chig Okonkwo led Commanders’ receivers with 6 receptions on 7 targets (85%, ADOT 5.4 yds), and finished a close second to Van Jefferson with 57 receiving yards. He was the Commanders’ fourth-most productive receiver at a respectable 1.63 Y/RR. Colson Yankoff caught his lone target for 6 yds. The other two TEs were used primarily as blockers. John Bates received a team-high 82.2 run blocking grade; while Ben Sinnott received a sub par 48.0. LT Brandon Coleman had a rough game in pass protection, allowing 1 sack, 1 QB hit and 2 hurries. His 9.8% pressure rate is about twice the acceptable rate for OTs. His 68.4 run blocking grade was the highest on the OL. To cap off the up and down performance, Brandon was flagged for 2 false starts. They were his 7 th and 8 th penalties this season. LG Chris Paul allowed just 1 QB hurry in pass protection (2.4% pressure rate). He received a season-high 60.0 run block grade, almost in the good range. Starting C Lucas Patrick left the game early with a concussion. He had not allowed a pressure in 13 pass blocking reps. Rookie Matt Gulbin replaced Patrick and took a beating from the Ram’s pass rushers. He allowed 1 sack, 1 QB hit and 1 hurry in 28 pass blocking snaps. His 10.7% pressure rate in pass protection is off the charts for interior blockers. His 57.3 run blocking grade was almost decent. RG Sam Cosmi allowed 1 QB hurry in pass protection (2.4% pressure rate). His 50.9 run blocking grade was his second-lowest of the season. Cosmi was penalized 10 yds for holding in the 2 nd quarter. RT Josh Conerly Jr took the brunt of the Rams’ edge rush. He allowed 1 QB hit and 5 hurries, resulting in the highest pressure rate on the OL (14.6%), which is saying something when two of his teammates were in double digits. He posted a 48.4 run block grade, his third-lowest of the season. DEFENSE The Rams did a great job of keeping the Commanders’ pass rush in check. As usual, K’Lavon Chaisson led the edge rushers in pressure rate, but only managed to generate pressure on 11.8% of pass rush attempts. Chaisson made 2 tackles, 1 assist and 1 forced fumble. He contributed to 3 defensive stops. Joshua Josephs only saw the field for 18 defensive snaps. He recorded 1 tackle and 1 hurry in the pass rush (8.3% pressure rate). Odafe Oweh recorded 1 QB hit and 1 hurry in the pass rush (7.7% pressure rate). One week after one of his best games with the Commanders, Dorance Armstrong failed to record a single stat against the Rams. NT Shy Tuttle recorded 1 tackle for loss and 3 assists and 1 hurry in the pass rush. DE Charles Omenihu made 1 tackle and 2 assists. In the pass rush, he generated 1 QB hit and 1 hurry. He contributed to 2 run stops (11.1% run stop rate). In his first game back from injury, Johnny Newton made 1 tackle and 2 assists, resulting in 1 stop. He generated a 1 QB hurry in the pass rush (11.1% pressure rate). Ricky Barber was elevated from the practice squad for this game. While only playing 15 defensive snaps, he managed to record 1 tackle and 1 tackle assist, with 1 stop. Deatrich Wise made 1 tackle assist, contributing to a stop. He generated 1 QB hurry in the pass rush (7.1% pressure rate). Tim Settle’s only statistical output was 1 QB hurry in the pass rush. Frankie Luvu led the team in tackling, with 7 tackles, including 2 TFL. Luvu contributed to a…

title: NFL Week 10 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips
summary: Patriots vs. Lions in Germany? Kirk Cousins' return to Minnesota? There are 13 more games in Week 10, and we have picks, predictions and more for all of them.
full_text:
Week 10 of the 2026 NFL season is here. The trade deadline came and went, with some surprising moves. QB Kirk Cousins is expected to be the Vikings' starting quarterback once again, the Chiefs added WR Josh Downs and ... RB  Jonathan Taylor is still in Indianapolis. A few teams added and others subtracted from their rosters. So, now it's time to dive back into the games.

 We're here to get you ready for the action. First, our NFL Nation reporters take you inside the locker room with the best thing they heard this week, and ESPN Research provides a key stat to know. Then, analytics writer Aaron Schatz makes a bold prediction for each matchup, fantasy analyst Eric Moody shares fantasy football intel and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado hits betting insights for each contest. We also have Football Power Index (FPI) game projections, and Maldonado, Moody and Schatz all give us final score picks for every game.

 Let's get into the full Week 10 slate, which culminates with a "Monday Night Football" matchup between the Chargers and Ravens on ESPN . (Game times are Sunday unless otherwise noted, and all odds are via DraftKings.)

 
 Jump to a matchup: 
 NE-DET | BUF-NYJ | CAR-NO 
 JAX-TEN | KC-ATL | MIA-IND 
 MIN-GB | HOU-CLE | SEA-LV 
 LAR-ARI | SF-DAL | PIT-CIN 
 LAC-BAL 

 Thursday: WSH-NYG 
 Bye: CHI , DEN , PHI , TB 

 
 

 What ESPN Analytics says ... 
 

 

 
 

 Patriots (5-4) at Lions (6-2)  in Munich 
 9:30 a.m. ET | Fox | DET -2.5 (51.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Patriots: New England is hoping to rebound from a poor defensive effort last week. Coordinator Zak Kuhr said CB Christian Gonzalez had some plays he would want back, but also said there were other plays where he could have been the closest defender because of breakdowns elsewhere. Kuhr acknowledged that very little went right for the defense but thought the unit took steps Wednesday in a spirited practice that featured better communication and connectivity. Kuhr added that the team's belief in Gonzalez hasn't wavered. -- Mike Reiss 

 What we're hearing on the Lions: It's not every day that the Lions are selected to play in an international game. In fact, it hasn't happened since 2015, so this is a huge deal for the franchise. WR Amon-Ra St. Brown 's mother, Miriam, hails from Germany, and he frequently visited the country as a child. This will be a new experience for coach Dan Campbell. "As far as I've been across the pond is London, and that was for [a game]," Campbell said. "And I already mentioned, I had an extra pair of underwear and socks and that was it, all right. And a toothbrush, but that's as far as I've been over there." -- Eric Woodyard 

 Stat to know: Lions QB Jared Goff has had consecutive games with fewer than 200 passing yards for just the second time over the past five seasons. -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: Patriots QB Drake Maye will not throw an interception against the Lions. His 11 interceptions this season are the second most in the league. In general, about 20% of passes defensed turn into interceptions. It's been a little lower leaguewide this season (16%). For Maye, it has been 34%. So he has been unlucky and shouldn't be as interception prone going forward. -- Schatz 

 

 Injuries: Patriots | Lions 

 Fantasy nugget: Corey Kiner could be the Patriots' lead RB against the Lions. Rhamondre Stevenson is expected to miss the game with a knee injury , and  TreVeyon Henderson  has been ruled out . Kiner has topped 50 rushing yards in three of his past five games despite playing a reserve role. Detroit is a difficult matchup, allowing the second-fewest fantasy points per game to RBs. However, Kiner could see enough volume to be a viable flex option. See Week 10 rankings . -- Moody 

 Betting insight: The Patriots have failed to cover four straight games, tied for the NFL's longest active streak and their longest since a five-game stretch in 2024. Detroit can keep that going. New England allows 10.6 yards per pass attempt against play-action, which Goff uses constantly. St. Brown can attack the slot, while New England's battered offensive line leaves Maye dodging pressure. Read more . -- Maldonado 

 Maldonado's pick: Lions 28, Patriots 23 
 Moody's pick: Lions 31, Patriots 24 
 Schatz's pick: Patriots 27, Lions 24 
 FPI prediction: DET, 52.6% (by an average of 0.7 points)

 

 Matchup must-reads: Pats' Stevenson expected to miss time with knee tendon issue 

 
 

 Bills (7-1) at Jets (2-7) 
 1 p.m. ET | CBS | BUF -8.5 (50.5 O/U) 

 What we're hearing on the Bills: Coming off a short week following "Monday Night Football," the Bills are still easing LT Dion Dawkins and LG Alec Anderson back into the lineup. But the Bills are plenty aware of Jets coach Aaron Glenn's aggressive tendencies and standout rookie edge rusher  David Bailey 's recent hot streak. Coach Joe Brady and offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael said they'll have to be aware of where Bailey lines up every play, and the task of keeping him out of the backfield is urgent: "He's already a star right now," Brady says, "but he's going to be a problem for a lot of years." -- Nick Suss 

 What we're hearing on the Jets: The spiraling defense has allowed 32 points per game over the team's current four-game losing streak. Glenn said he's "looking at everything" in an attempt to halt the slide. He doesn't have many personnel options, though it appears that disgruntled edge rusher Will McDonald IV will get more playing time than usual. The Jets have another long interception drought brewing -- five straight games without a pick, 15 shy of the league record (set by them just prior to the current five-game slump). -- Rich Cimini 

 Stat to know: Bills RB James Cook III has had 75-plus rushing yards in seven straight games, the longest active streak in the NFL and the longest by a Bills player since Travis Henry in 2003 (eight). -- ESPN Research 

 Bold prediction: Jets WR Garrett Wilson ( concussion ) will return and set a season high with at least 110 receiving yards. Buffalo currently ranks 27th in DVOA (Defense-adjusted Value Over Average) against WR1s, and Wilson is the Jets' clear top option. -- Schatz 

 

 Injuries: Bills | Jets 

 Fantasy nugget: Jets RB Breece Hall returned from a five-game absence last week and led the Jets' backfield with 18 touches and 11.7 fantasy points. Before a quad injury, Hall had been the clear lead back on early downs, but he split that work much more evenly with Braelon Allen in Week 9.  Tennessee will wear its "Music City"-inspired combination against the Jacksonville Jaguars . It includes a two-tone blue color palette with a Titans-blue lid and navy uniform. The numbers are reminiscent of a neon sign, a nod to those that run through Nashville. "Music City" runs across the chest, while six rhythmic stripes run down the side, similar to strings on a guitar.

The shield shoulder patch is black and midnight purple, while "darkness there and nothing more" runs on the inside collar -- a reference to a quote from Edgar Allen Poe's "The Raven."

 Monochromatic alternates are popular around the rest of the league. The Cincinnati Bengals will wear their "White Bengal" helmet with all-white uniforms, first introduced in 2022, against the Pittsburgh Steelers . Cincinnati has gone 5-1 in the white helmets since they debuted in 2022. It's "Alpha Dawg" week for the Cleveland Browns , who will don all-brown against the Houston Texans .

title: 2026 NFL midseason report: Questions, stats for all 32 teams entering second half
summary: The 2026 NFL season has hit the midway point. Here's what to watch in the second half, key QB stats and fantasy nuggets for all 32 teams.
full_text:
Nine weeks of the 2026 NFL season have passed. Some teams are riding high, while others are grasping for wins.

 Much of what we believed we knew when it all began in September has been validated -- but lots of surprises, blockbuster trades and injuries have changed the course of our early-season predictions. 

 AFC South-leading Jacksonville went all-in on the defensive side with a trio of trades before the deadline this week, while John Harbaugh has the NFC East-leading New York Giants believing they hired the right man. No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza has yet to take the reins in Las Vegas but will this week after another big trade ; there's not a single rookie who has stood out enough so far to say that the race for ROY isn't wide open. The NFC North remains the strongest division halfway through the season, while both Super Bowl participants have looked shaky of late. Of note, neither Seattle (11) nor New England (16) was ranked in the FPI top 10 at this point last season.

 With that in mind, ESPN's 32 NFL team reporters took part in a midseason reset. Here, they lay out what they've learned through the first nine games and frame what's to come over the final nine weeks and beyond. Teams are ranked below by where each stands in ESPN's Football Power Index (FPI) rankings, and each club's current odds to win the division are also included as well as Eric Moody's non-QB fantasy football nuggets.

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 

 

 

 
 
 San Francisco 49ers 
 FPI rank:  1 
 Chances to make the playoffs:  99.3% 
 Chances to win their division:  94.6%

 First-half storyline: The 49ers have jumped to a 7-1 start despite more injuries to key players, including to DE Nick Bosa (calf) and WR Mike Evans (Achilles tendinitis). But the Niners have again overcome those issues to find themselves in the driver's seat for the NFC's No. 1 seed with wins against three of the last four teams in the 2025 playoffs.

 
 QB stat to know: Brock Purdy leads the NFL with a QBR of 82.5 and is firmly in the mix for the NFL's Most Valuable Player award. Perhaps more important given the other injury issues is that Purdy has started and finished all eight games, providing stability at the game's most important position.

 

 
 Second-half storyline: Despite the hot start, the 49ers believe they can be better. Some of that will depend on health, but San Francisco has five starters in their first or second seasons -- and even more youngsters in key roles. If those players continue to develop, it could push the Niners to another level. -- Nick Wagoner 

 Fantasy nugget: Brock Purdy started the season averaging 27.0 fantasy PPG in the first three games. Since then, he has scored 18.1 fantasy PPG and has topped 20 points just once. He has the fourth-toughest remaining QB schedule, with games against the Vikings, Seahawks, Rams and Chiefs still on tap. It may be worth putting him on the trade block this week. -- Moody 

 

 

 
 Buffalo Bills 
 FPI rank: 2 
 Chances to make the playoffs:  99.8% 
 Chances to win their division:  96.3%

 First-half storyline: Historic offense, problematic defense: The Josh Allen -Joe Brady partnership is a huge argument for continuity, with the Bills scoring at rates comparable to those of the best offenses in NFL history. But coordinator Jim Leonhard's defense, especially the secondary, is leaky and still figuring out communication issues far too late in the season.

 
 QB stat to know: Allen has maintained a league-leading and career-best yards per attempt average (8.6) despite an injury that kept his best deep threat (WR DJ Moore ) out of the lineup for the better part of four games. Even if it's not Brady's primary emphasis, the 2026 Bills are more explosive than they were even in Allen's best years.

 
 Second-half storyline: The Thanksgiving to Christmas gauntlet: From Thanksgiving Day through Christmas Day, the Bills will play five consecutive games against contenders: Kansas City, at New England, at Green Bay, Chicago, at Denver. It's the toughest stretch of the season at the most important point of the season, and should decide whether the Bills hold on as AFC Super Bowl favorites. -- Nick Suss 

 Fantasy nugget: DJ Moore has a 26% target share, 41% air yard share and 14.3 fantasy PPG in his four full games. That is high-end WR2 production, but he will be tested to maintain it, as he has the toughest remaining fantasy schedule for WRs. -- Moody 

 

 

 
 Cincinnati Bengals 
 FPI rank:  3 
 Chances to make the playoffs:  98.6% 
 Chances to win their division:  79.5%

 First-half storyline: Joe Burrow has officially found his groove, and the offense has never been better. The Bengals are third in points per drive (2.82), first in third-down conversion percentage (53.6%) and in fewest number of drives without a first down (18.3%). The engine that is built to lead the team is doing exactly that.

 
 QB stat to know: Burrow has been otherworldly at stretching the field vertically, which is as much a credit to Burrow as it is to his star receivers -- Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins . On throws of 15 air yards or more, Burrow has a 99.3 QBR and a whopping 18.1% completion percentage over expectation, per ESPN Research.

 
 Second-half storyline: Can the offense continue its torrid pace? The offense has masked the defensive inconsistencies that have popped up in various moments. Third downs and allowing big rushing plays have been issues. But if the Bengals can keep forcing turnovers and keep their defensive red zone efficiency high (currently fifth), that might be enough. -- Ben Baby 

 Fantasy nugget: The Bengals have arguably the best passing attack in the NFL at the moment. Joe Burrow is the fantasy QB2, while Tee Higgins and Ja'Marr Chase are both top-five WRs. That will be tested as the Bengals have the seventh-toughest remaining fantasy schedule for QBs and third-toughest for WRs. Meanwhile, struggling Chase Brown has the third- best fantasy RB schedule. -- Moody 

 

 

 
 Jacksonville Jaguars 
 FPI rank:  4 
 Chances to make the playoffs:  98.8% 
 Chances to win their division:  93.4%

 First-half storyline: The Jaguars are beating teams at a historic pace. They have four victories by 23 or more points, which is the most in a single season in franchise history. They're also the fifth team since 1999 with four victories by 23 or more points in the first eight games of the season -- three of the previous four teams that did that reached the Super Bowl, per ESPN Research.

 
 QB stat to know: Trevor Lawrence has the NFL's lowest off-target percentage at 9.2%, which is by far the best percentage of his career (15% in 2025 was his previous best). Coach Liam Coen has praised Lawrence's footwork, which was the first thing he worked to fix in the spring before his first season as coach in Jacksonville in 2025, as a reason for his improved accuracy.

 
 Second-half storyline: The Jaguars must keep the pass rush from being a liability. They are seventh in pressure rate but have only 16 sacks -- just four ahead of last-place Miami. Edge rushers Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker only have a combined five sacks. That's not going to be good enough against Caleb Williams , Aaron Rodgers , C.J. Stroud and Dak Prescott , who are all left on their schedule. -- Mike DiRocco 

 

 Fantasy nugget: Bhayshul Tuten is 15th among RBs in fantasy PPG and is third in the NFL in forced missed tackles rate. Tuten leads the Jags in goal-line carries and has scored three of their four goal-line TDs. In fact, he and Kenneth Walker III are the only RBs in the NFL with at least three rushing and receiving touchdowns this season.  -- Moody

title: Is Chuba Hubbard the biggest X factor to spark a Panthers turnaround?
summary: Meet Carolina's team captain, a locker room leader and a relentless running back who is "chasing greatness myself."
full_text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- Chuba Hubbard  knows that no one is perfect. But that hasn't stopped the Carolina Panthers ' running back from chasing perfection. And after a forgettable, injury-marred 2025 campaign, during which he lost his starting job after a career season in 2024, the team captain is leading the backfield again, and he's perhaps better than ever.

 "I pride myself in hard work and staying consistent in knowing what I can do and trying to bring my best every single day, so it's more so just fighting for excellence and fighting to be perfect in every way possible," Hubbard told ESPN.

 Hubbard, 27, signed a four-year, $33.2 million contract extension during his breakout 2024 campaign, when he rushed for 1,195 yards and produced 11 total touchdowns in 15 games. Through eight games in 2026, he has rushed for 619 yards and produced seven total touchdowns, bouncing back as the Panthers have struggled to find consistency almost everywhere else during a three-game losing streak and a 3-5 start.

 

 But those numbers don't tell the complete story of Hubbard's value. He's talented, sure, but his true worth is as a tone-setter for the organization.

 Though he was selected by the franchise, while Matt Rhule was the coach, in the fourth round of the 2021 NFL draft, Hubbard has established himself as the standard-bearer for the Dave Canales era over the past three seasons. And with Carolina fighting to maintain its position atop the NFC South, his value has become apparent, if not paramount, to the team's ability to recalibrate its season.

 "What I love about Chuba is that the things that we talk about wanting to be as an organization, he represents those in spades," Canales said. "His preparation, the way that he works, the way I have to kind of reel him in and call him back a little bit because he goes so hard."

 Hubbard could be the X factor who wills Carolina to a win Sunday at the Caesars Superdome ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ), where the Panthers haven't won since the 2022 season. Hubbard, who has 70.8% of the team's carries this season, will face the New Orleans Saints , who have one of the league's worst rushing defenses (ranked 29th). A win could reignite Carolina's hopes of securing consecutive division titles for the first time since the franchise owned the NFC South crown from 2013 to 2015.

 According to those who know him best, Hubbard is ready to shoulder that burden, not only because of who he is as a player, but also because of who he is as a person and a leader in the locker room.

 

 Chuba Hubbard's style 'keeps a defense honest' and could bode well in New Orleans 

 Hubbard entered Week 10 with the 10th-most rushing yards in the NFL. He has played one fewer game than five of the backs who are in front of him on that list, and three of those playmakers ( Derrick Henry with 689, Jonathan Taylor at 656 and Javonte Williams at 629) have fewer than 70 more yards than Hubbard.

 This week, the Panthers' top back will get an opportunity to make up ground on the rushing leader list against the Saints. New Orleans allows 133.9 rushing yards per game and 4.52 yards per carry. With New Orleans also struggling against the pass (ranked 28th with 236.6 passing yards allowed per game), Hubbard could take advantage of quarterback Bryce Young 's passing threat against potentially lighter tackle boxes.

 Hubbard's ability to gain momentum throughout a game has made him a steady presence in an otherwise erratic offense. And his north-south rushing style should be a challenge for a Saints defense that has struggled to bring down ball carriers.

 Through eight games, Hubbard has averaged 26.5 rushing yards in the first half of games. He has nearly doubled that number with a 50.9 rushing-yards average in the second half. Hubbard also has 110 rushing yards over expected (RYOE), defined as the difference between actual rushing yards and expected rushing yards on a series of plays, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. That total ranks sixth in the league entering Week 10.

 "That aligns with who Chuba is as a player, a person," Panthers offensive coordinator Brad Idzik said recently. "He's going to outwork you. He's going to outlast you. He's going to out-prepare you. ... Whereas some people wear down throughout the game, it feels like he gets stronger, because he's prepared for that."

 

 Hubbard's lopsided first- and second-half splits are partially due to Young airing out the ball consistently in the first half, which is wearing down opposing defenses, particularly in the second and third levels. The other part is that Hubbard is fresh down the stretch of games, and can bulldoze past (and through) defenders. He has 16 explosive runs (10 yards or more gained), which ranks eighth in the NFL.

 Hubbard "keeps a defense honest," said a pro scout of an NFC team that played the Panthers in the first half of the season. "Good size and vision to run between the tackles; enough speed and agility to be used on outside runs. ... You can't put him in one box [with] what he does well and what he doesn't do well."

 ESPN NFL analyst Dan Orlovsky said Hubbard has a "really strong lower half, is a smart pass catcher in space [and he] runs with energy." Hubbard's vision and patience help the Panthers stay ahead of the sticks. Historically, he is not the type of player to lose yardage on a carry because of his ability to read blocks, break tackles and power to -- at worst -- the line of scrimmage.

 "You're never going to have too many zero-[yard] runs with him, or negative runs; that's the thing I like about him," Panthers run game coordinator Harold Goodwin said last week. "There's really no perfect run every play, but he creates something on every play, so just as long as we get on people [with blocking], he's always going to come out with positive yards."

 Hubbard has also improved considerably as a pass blocker and receiver throughout his career. He had seven drops on 37 targets as a rookie in 2021, while mostly filling in for All-Pro running back Christian McCaffrey . Hubbard also had a rough three-year stretch from a blitz-pickup perspective from 2022 to 2024.

 Those third-down woes impacted his playing time and the fan base's perception of him. So, the Edmonton, Alberta, native worked to improve himself by "chopping the tree every single day."

 

 

 Preparation is key for 27-year-old RB who 'wants to be able to do everything' 

 Hubbard has a relentless training regimen, which includes what Idzik calls "the most consistent pre- and post-practice routines I've been around."

 Hubbard spends roughly 30 minutes after practice working on the Jugs machine daily, an exercise several teammates, including tight end Tommy Tremble , have embraced over the years.

 In the five seasons since his rookie campaign, Hubbard has caught 141 passes for 965 yards and six touchdowns -- with 10 total drops (just one this season), according to ESPN Research -- as a result of the tedious steps he takes throughout the week.

 According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Hubbard gave up six sacks and 41 pressures in his first four seasons. He has allowed just nine pressures and zero sacks in the 23 games since that stretch.

 "I want to be able to do everything, from blocking to catching to running the ball," Hubbard said. "Obviously, that's something that I had to work on a lot and obviously felt the criticism. I told myself, 'I would be wrong if I didn't fix this thing.' Like, I'd be wrong if I didn't put my best foot forward to be the best I can be, especially for myself and my team."

 Hubbard has still had ups and downs on the field regardless of his preparation.

 Last season, he was effectively benched after a lingering calf injury soured the start of his 2025 season. Fellow running back Rico Dowdle -- now in Pittsburgh -- was signed to a one-year deal to team up with Hubbard, and instead of serving as Hubbard's backup, Dowdle became the primary back throughout the majority of the Panthers' NFC South…
