full_text:
It's midseason awards time. I'm here to hand out my ballot for the first half of the 2026 NFL season . And in a year that has felt dominated by parity and very few players or teams separating from the pack, it wasn't easy to pick favorites. There are multiple legitimate contenders to win every single award through nine weeks, running all the way from Most Valuable Player (where I counted six players who had a legitimate argument) to Comeback Player of the Year (where three future Hall of Famers came back from season-ending injuries and immediately looked like their old selves).

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 As always, these are my picks for who I feel should win each of these awards after the first half of the season as opposed to predictions for who the voters are likely to actually select by the end of the year. I place a priority on availability, so players who have sat out more than a game or so because of injury will find it difficult to compete with players who have answered the call each and every weekend. And naturally, I'm using healthy amounts of data and what I've seen watching All-22 film every week to inform my choices here.

 Let's begin with the rookies and others before wrapping up with my MVP rankings and my midseason All-Pro team.

 

 
 Jump to an award: 
 DROY | OROY |  Coach of the Year 
 Comeback Player of the Year 
 Protector of the Year 
 DPOY | OPOY | MVP  | All-Pro roster 

 
 

 Defensive Rookie of the Year 
 My top pick five weeks ago : Arvell Reese 

 After the offense-heavy draft classes in 2024 and 2025, this has been a very fun crop of defensive rookies, driven by the players at the very top. There were no sure things, but we're seeing a lot of players who had questions about their fit in a defense or as every-down options thrive. The 49ers' and Chiefs' first-year defenders in particular have been exciting to watch, although Mansoor Delane 's shoulder injury has kept the top-drafted cornerback in the class from getting on the field often enough to compete for this award, while defensive tackle  Gracen Halton sustained a season-ending broken ankle for the 49ers.

 I was left with five contenders for three spots. Jacob Rodriguez has been ever present at linebacker for the Dolphins and has been a very good run defender while wearing the green dot for Miami as a rookie. The Bengals were able to isolate Rodriguez in coverage for a couple of touchdowns earlier this season , but he has generally had the athleticism to compete there against running backs and tight ends.

 

 And though  Brandon Cisse 's season got off to a tough start against Justin Jefferson , the Packers cornerback has improved. He has been surprisingly impactful along the line of scrimmage, creating problems as a blitzer and making quick reads and sure tackles on screens. He has been one of the biggest reasons the Packers -- whose outside cornerbacks struggled last season -- have been able to withstand the absence of Micah Parsons .

 

 3. Sonny Styles , LB, Washington Commanders 
 Of course, I have to start any conversation about Styles by mentioning what might have been one of the single most impressive highlights I saw from any player in the first half of the season -- when he  obliterated   Saquon Barkley in pass protection. It hasn't been an isolated moment for the Commanders linebacker, either, as we're repeatedly seeing his physicality and athleticism impact blockers and draw eyes in pass protection.

 He has also been a quick study in coverage over the middle of the field, showing a real comfort with understanding route distributions and passing receivers off to avoid creating the voids that offenses try to exploit. It has been a frustrating season for the Commanders, but Styles looks as if he's going to be an essential part of the defense moving forward.

 

 2. David Bailey , Edge, New York Jets 
 Bailey is long and athletic, and we saw those traits last week , when it very briefly appeared that he had injured Patrick Mahomes . Bailey terrorized Chiefs tackle Jaylon Moore for two strip sacks in a four-play span, and he's tied with Fred Warner for a league-leading five strip sacks so far this season.

 Bailey has 7.5 sacks overall, 12 quarterback hits and 10 tackles for loss. Some of those numbers are a little inflated; Bailey got his first career sack in the opener against the Titans on a play on which he didn't touch Cam Ward as the quarterback ran out of bounds, then another as Jordan Love slid in front of the rookie edge rusher. But don't let that mask his impact on a down-by-down basis. Bailey is second among all players with a 20.6% pressure rate and 20th in quick pressure rate at 5.7%. Teams haven't doubled Bailey very often, but that's going to change in the second half. He's already one of the league's most unstoppable pass rushers.

 

 1. Arvell Reese , LB/Edge, New York Giants 
 Picking between Bailey and Reese is unfair. I leaned Reese if only because he has been two impactful players in one this season. As an off-ball linebacker, Reese has been all over the place for a Giants team that has been better against the run this season, even after trading  Dexter Lawrence II . Reese has made tackles on 15.3% of his snaps, the eighth-highest rate in the league. He has given up an  81.3 passer rating in coverage , a very credible number for a veteran linebacker, let alone a rookie just getting his feet wet at this level.

 And then there's Reese's side quest as a devastating force on blitzes. Despite rushing the quarterback only about 11 times per game, Reese already has 4.5 sacks and 14 pressures. His 10.2% quick pressure rate would be the second-best mark in the NFL if he qualified. And the average Reese pressure comes after 2.44 seconds, the fifth fastest among players with 10 pressures or more.

 

 The Giants are already building pass-rush packages around Reese, like when they isolated him  against Eagles guard  Landon Dickerson last week , with one of the league's highest-paid interior linemen struggling to even slow Reese down on one of his three sacks. Philly decided to leave Reese completely unblocked for another. Reese was also the best player on the field earlier this season in a  win over the Cardinals , making the difference in swinging a close game New York's way.

 Reese vs. Bailey is going to be a conversation in bars around New York and New Jersey for a long time.

 

 

 Offensive Rookie of the Year 
 My top pick five weeks ago : Denzel Boston 

 All you need to know about the offensive side, meanwhile, is that Fernando Mendoza instantly became the betting favorite to take home this hardware after the Kirk Cousins trade Tuesday afternoon . There are plenty of rookies who have flashed with a nice week or two, but very few have sustained a significant level of play over the first half. As a result, my feelings here head in a somewhat surprising direction at the top.

 

 3. Carnell Tate , WR, Tennessee Titans 
 Sitting out last week's game against the Bengals (and its high-scoring 43-36 result) probably hurt Tate's chances of climbing to the top of the award ballot at midseason, but after a slow start, the Ohio State product is settling in as the focal point of the Titans' passing game. He leads all rookies in averaging 2.2 yards per route run, which is right in line with what Justin Jefferson (2.2) and Tetairoa McMillan (2.1) are averaging this season. And though Tate has only one touchdown, Cam Ward has missed him on at least two other potential scores.

 

 2. Denzel Boston , WR, Cleveland Browns 
 Boston leads all rookies with 507 receiving yards, owing in part to the fact that he has run 301 routes, the seventh most of any player in the NFL. Boston has been the big-play provider for the Browns, with his three catches of 50 or more yards tied with Christian Watson of the Packers for the most in the league. His 55-yard touchdown against the Bucs was the best of the bunch, with Boston breaking three tackles…

title: NFL trade deadline grades: Deals for Kirk Cousins, Josh Downs, Ryan Neuzil
summary: Was getting Kirk Cousins a home run for the Vikings? Did the Chiefs make a smart move to pick up Josh Downs?
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals from the 2026 trade deadline , which passed Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for all 17 deals, including three Jaguars trades from Monday, three quarterback moves for teams in need and multiple deals involving at least one first-round pick.

 Editor's note: The Broncos announced via social media early Thursday morning that the trade to acquire Daiyan Henley from the Chargers "will not be finalized," so the grade for that deal has been removed below. 

 

 
 Jump to a trade: 
 Neuzil/Vorhees |  Downs | Hooker 
 Cousins  |  Allen  |  Davis 
 Godchaux  |  Cisco  |  Bates  |  Brissett 
 Simmons  |  Buckner  |  Nelson  |  Harrison 
 Jurgens  |  Porter | McCarthy 

 
 

 

 Falcons trade C Neuzil to Ravens for G Vorhees 
 Ravens get: C Ryan Neuzil 
 Falcons get: G Andrew Vorhees , 2028 sixth-round pick

 Falcons grade: C- 
 Ravens grade: B+

 The Ravens traded for their second center of this deadline season, with Neuzil heading to Baltimore for Vorhees and a late-round pick. It is a surprising and, at first glance, somewhat confusing deal.

 Neuzil is a solid center who ranks in the 57th and 50th percentile in pass block win rate and run block win rate at the position, respectively. He is in the last year of his contract.

 It's a little hard to know each team's plan. Cam Jurgens has been struggling since the Ravens acquired him a little over a month ago. Is Neuzil coming in to start over him? Is one of them moving to guard? Or is this just a pure value play?

 The Falcons have so much cap space in 2027 that they are likely to be very active in free agency and therefore unlikely to receive compensatory picks for players lost. Did the Falcons know they weren't going to bring back Neuzil and dealt him to avoid losing him for nothing? That's possible, though I would have thought they would have managed more of a return. But maybe that's what attracted the Ravens -- they saw this as a value play that could net them a profit in terms of compensatory picks with upside that Neuzil could help them now and in the future.

 I don't mind that for Baltimore, especially since the Jurgens deal already is looking like a mistake. But it's a tougher sell for the Falcons. I would much rather try to re-sign Neuzil to a long-term deal (perhaps they did). If they were going to trade Neuzil, was this really the best they could get? And though the Falcons are hardly contenders, this certainly won't help quarterback Michael Penix Jr . down the stretch.

 

 Backup Corey Levin will presumably start going forward. Vorhees figures to be a depth guard for the Falcons as he was for the Ravens. -- Walder 

 

 

 Colts trade WR Downs to Chiefs 
 Chiefs get: WR Josh Downs , 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick

 Chiefs grade: B+ 
 Colts grade: B+

 Downs is free! The slot receiver is out of Indianapolis and now has a chance to be a major part of the Chiefs' offense down the stretch and, perhaps, during a playoff run.

 Downs has earned 354 receiving yards on 33 receptions this season (1.2 yards per route run) but has recorded 1.7 yards per route run over the course of his career. But as any fantasy football die-hard will tell you, Downs has much more potential than that.

 

 Over his four seasons, Downs has a 68 open score in ESPN's receiver scores , which evaluate a receiver's ability to get open on all routes -- not only the ones when he is targeted. And that 68 score means Downs is well above average. Though this has hardly been a guarantee for past Chiefs receivers, it is possible that playing with Patrick Mahomes will unlock a higher level of production from Downs.

 Kansas City is back to being a contender -- the Chiefs entered Tuesday with a 96% chance to reach the playoffs and a 7% chance to win the Super Bowl -- but their offense hasn't felt as if it has reached its maximum potential. The Chiefs rank only eighth in EPA per dropback but have been able to outperform that because of the rushing success of  Kenneth Walker III .

 Rashee Rice (35%) and Xavier Worthy (20%) spend time in the slot, but I expect those numbers will drop with Downs, who aligned in the slot 51% of the time in Indianapolis this season, now on the team. Over his career, Rice's numbers have been slightly worse in the slot (2.3 yards per route run) compared with when he's lined up outside or elsewhere (2.8).

 The cost here is similar to what the Seahawks gave up last year for Rashid Shaheed who, like Downs, was in a contract year. Perhaps the Chiefs will re-sign Downs as the Seahawks did with Shaheed but if not, they should be in line for a likely compensatory pick given that Kansas City does not have much cap room for in 2027. Given the Chiefs' need to augment the offense and status as a true contender, I think this is a worthwhile addition.

 

 As for the Colts, while I wouldn't have been opposed to them signing Downs to a long-term deal given his age (25) and talent, dealing him is quite logical. They are in the midst of a teardown, and if Downs left via free agency, they would not recoup this much value in a compensatory pick -- if they even got one. -- Walder 

 

 

 Titans trade S Hooker to Bills 
 Bills get: S Amani Hooker , 2027 fifth-round pick 
 Titans get: 2027 second-round pick

 Bills grade: C+ 
 Titans grade: A-

 As the Bills push for a title run, safety was an obvious place for an upgrade. I thought the answer might be Jessie Bates III , but the Jaguars -- arguably Buffalo's biggest threat in the AFC -- traded for the former Falcons safety  Monday.

 After the team released C.J. Gardner-Johnson last week, Damar Hamlin was left playing next to Cole Bishop , with Geno Stone as the third safety. In Hooker, the Titans upgrade from Hamlin and pick up a player who has been having an impactful season in Tennessee.

 

 Hooker has recorded five interceptions and six passes defensed this season with the Titans, good enough to have the sixth-best EPA allowed on targets among safeties. All current metrics on safeties are quite noisy, but some of the others are not as strong: 1.0 yards per coverage snap this season and last, and positive EPA allowed in 2025.

 The Bills will be getting him on a value contract, as they will be on the hook for the rest of Hooker's roughly $8.9 million in salary and per game roster bonuses this year, and then will be slated to pay him a non-guaranteed $10.3 million in 2027 and $13.5 million in 2028, per OverTheCap.com . That's less than Hooker would make on the open market, I believe, though not free.

 

 So Hooker is an upgrade at a position of need for a Super Bowl-contending team and will save them a few million dollars per year relative to the market. But is that worth a second-round pick? It strikes me as rich. Hooker is a good player but not a star -- he has never been a Pro Bowl selection or All-Pro and only snuck into Jeremy Fowler's NFL evaluator survey of top safeties in the "also receiving votes" category. As a result, the compensation here is a bit steep. -- Walder 

 

 

 Raiders trade QB Cousins to Vikings 
 Vikings get: QB Kirk Cousins 
 Raiders get: 2027 third-round pick

 Vikings grade: A 
 Raiders grade: B+

 The Vikings were in the unusual position of being Super Bowl contenders who desperately needed a quarterback. And Tuesday was essentially the last day they could get one.

 Kyler Murray is hurt and clearly not a fit in Kevin O'Connell's offense.…

title: It's a battle for the AFC North: Steelers at Bengals Week 10 primer
summary: Aaron Rodgers and Joe Burrow and their 6-2 teams face off Sunday night, and Ben Baby and Brooke Pryor break down the matchup.
full_text:
Pittsburgh Steelers defensive coordinator Patrick Graham arrived at his news conference a few minutes late Monday afternoon.

 "Sorry about that," he said as he stepped behind the lectern. " Tee Higgins , Joe Burrow , [ Ja'Marr] Chase , a lot of guys."

 He laughed and shook his head as a reporter asked if anything was different from their first matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals nearly two months earlier -- a 30-27 win in Week 3.

 "No, they're all out there," he said.

 It's a matchup that would give any defensive coordinator nightmares, and Sunday night in Cincinnati ( 8:20 ET, NBC ) the chess game between the Bengals' high-flying offense and the Steelers' stalwart, veteran-laden defense clashes again with high stakes.

 

 The winner of Sunday's rematch will move into first place in the AFC North . For the Steelers, a win will mean a crucial division sweep of the Bengals to maintain their tiebreak advantage. For the Bengals, a victory will even the 2026 series with the Steelers with three division games left -- including two against the frisky Cleveland Browns .

 "I love playing in primetime," Burrow said. "Some guys would rather play at 1 [p.m.]. I'd rather play every game [on] Sunday night, 'Monday Night Football.' I want to be able to showcase what we do and how hard we work and go and showcase what we can do to the world. And this is a big moment for it."

 Burrow, though, has never played in a home divisional primetime game. On the other side, the Steelers haven't won a road divisional primetime game since 2024.

 Since their September meeting, each team has lost once, and both enter the matchup riding a four-game winning streak. The Steelers are well-rested after a bye week, while the Bengals are recovering from a quick trip to Madrid, where they beat the Atlanta Falcons   34-17 . DraftKings has the Bengals as 3.5-point favorites.

 "We have a lot of positive energy going right now, and we got a big-time game, 'Sunday Night Football' in Cincinnati," Steelers coach Mike McCarthy said earlier this week. "It's going to be a great atmosphere, and we got a chance to sweep the Bengals and that's what you have to do in division games. You have to win these division games."

 Steelers reporter Brooke Pryor and Bengals reporter Ben Baby break down the big game.

 
 Burrow vs. Rodgers: One QB coming off a big win and another off bye. How does each respond? 

 Baby: Other NFL quarterbacks can only dream of the situation Burrow finds himself in -- mining through the finest details of his game that need to be improved.

 Because as of now, he's playing as well as ever in his seven-year career. In his past four games, he has thrown 16 touchdowns to just three interceptions. If one takes away drops and throwaways, Burrow is completing 82.2% of his passes.

 

 And yet, the misses linger. There was a throw last week against the Falcons that he wanted back.

 "I just hold myself to a high standard and learn from my mistakes," Burrow said.

 Cincinnati is aware of the rhythm Burrow is in and how that needs to be nurtured for the rest of the season.

 "When you find yourself in that place, you have to maintain the urgency to stay there because you don't just take that for granted," Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher said.

 Pryor: Aaron Rodgers grinned as he spoke to the media Wednesday in his first availability since getting a full week off for the Steelers' Week 9 bye.

 "I always look forward to it, and appreciate Mike's bye week schedules over the years," Rodgers said.

 McCarthy has a 12-6 career bye record, but Rodgers doesn't put too much stock in it.

 "I think that's one of those stats you can just find if you're looking for it," Rodgers said. "Obviously, there's a slight advantage in rest, but yeah, I just think that's an outlier stat, probably."

 Before the bye, Rodgers had his lowest passing output of the season in the Steelers' Week 8 win against the Browns, completing 52% of his attempts for 172 yards and an interception. For the season, Rodgers is averaging 6.5 air yards per attempt -- up from 5.9 in 2025 -- but he aired it out in the Week 3 meeting with the Bengals. He had two touchdown throws of 20-plus air yards in the victory (and just one such passing touchdown in all other seven games combined, per ESPN Research), and he averaged a season-high 8.6 yards per attempt.

 Rodgers, who is 2-0 in head-to-head matchups with Burrow, enters this primetime matchup with 180 career wins including playoffs, one away from tying former New Orleans Saints QB Drew Brees for fourth most since 1950.

 

 
 Which units have improved the most since these teams last played each other? 

 Baby: The offense. One of the pretenses the Bengals finally dropped midway through the season is that with Burrow at quarterback, there's no notion of a traditional offense.

 What happens on first-and-10 tells the full story. In those neutral situations, the Bengals were under center on 56.3% of those snaps at the start of the offensive sequence. Since then, that rate has plummeted to a mere 25.2%, good for the lowest rate in the NFL, per ESPN Research.

 Here's another fact that might surprise people: The Bengals like throwing the ball.

 Cincinnati is last in the NFL in rushing attempts (177) and rushes per game (22.1). When Burrow, Chase and Higgins are playing this well, one sticks with them.

 Pryor: The run game. Jaylen Warren exploded in the first matchup between these two teams, and the ground game has been on a roll since. With Rico Dowdle sidelined, Warren racked up 176 all-purpose yards in the Week 3 victory.

 "What 30 did in that game, that was kind of his stepping into the spotlight moment this season," Rodgers said Wednesday. "He was unbelievable. Just the amount of tackles that he forced, missed, just his vision, he was the catalyst behind that. So fortunately or unfortunately, he set the standard that day for himself, and he's lived up to it the last few weeks, and he's a dynamic player."

 Warren has eclipsed 100 rushing yards in three of the Steelers' five games since the Cincinnati win, including a season-high 143 in the team's most recent triumph against the Browns. The Steelers are averaging 145.7 rushing yards in their past three games.

 

 How does Pittsburgh halt the long game on the outside with Chase and Higgins? 

 Pryor: Say a prayer? Outside of divine intervention, though, the Steelers' best hope to limit deep shots to Chase and Higgins is through an effective pass rush. In Week 3, the Bengals relied on a quick passing game, and as a result, the Steelers' pass rush didn't get many opportunities to affect Burrow. The Steelers sacked Burrow just once when Derrick Harmon , who returned to practice this week but is still on injured reserve, brought the quarterback down late in the game.

 

 "At the end of the game we got them into some advantageous situations, and so when we did that, then we got our pass rush hitting home," Steelers defensive tackle Cameron Heyward said this week. "But it was just about staying patient in the game, and going into this game, we're not going to have as many shots, but when we get them, we got to make them count."

 The Steelers' secondary has been inconsistent in shutting down splash plays, and that has certainly been the case in previous matchups with Chase and Higgins. And if the Bengals go back to the quick pass formula, the Steelers have to be sure they have tacklers to limit the Bengals' explosiveness after the catch.

 Baby: Fortunately for Pittsburgh, it has perhaps the only solution that is currently helpful in stopping Cincinnati's explosive tandem -- a good defensive front. Throughout the week, Cincinnati talked about how when a team is able to be effective with four pass rushers, it leaves the other seven defenders on the field devoted to pass coverage.

 "If there's any team in the league who dictates that the defense should be devoting as much or all of their resources to coverage, it would…

title: NFC North: Bears win division? Cousins has Vikes in command?
summary: What will Kirk Cousins and Micah Parsons mean for the best division in football, or will the Bears hang on?
full_text:
No one in the NFL was on a bigger high coming out of last weekend than the Green Bay Packers .

 They trounced the defending AFC champion New England Patriots  45-27 and put together their best performance of the season to improve to 6-3.

 And then Packers coach Matt LaFleur killed the buzz: "The reality is this: We're in last place in our division right now."

 Such is life in the NFC North, the most victorious division in football, where the Chicago Bears are on top at 7-3, followed by the Detroit Lions (6-2), Minnesota Vikings (6-2) and Packers (6-3).

 The NFC North is the seventh division since 2002 with all four teams above .500 through Week 9, according to ESPN Research. It has the best combined record (25-9, 73.5 winning percentage) by any division in the first nine weeks of a season under the current division format, which began 24 years ago.

 

 The last time all four teams in a division had a winning record at this point in a season was 2023 with the AFC North. All four finished with winning records, and all but the Cincinnati Bengals (9-8) made the playoffs. The Baltimore Ravens made it to the AFC Championship Game.

 On the flip side of that was the 2022 AFC East, which also had every team with a winning record through Week 9 but had only two teams reach the playoffs, and neither advanced past the divisional round.

 ESPN's FPI gives the Bears the best shot at winning the division at 35.1%, ahead of the Vikings (29.7%), Lions (24.7%) and Packers (10.5%).

 So what's real and what's not in the NFC North? Reporters Courtney Cronin (Bears), Rob Demovsky (Packers), Kevin Seifert (Vikings) and Eric Woodyard (Lions) give their insight:

 

 

 Real or not: Acquiring  Kirk Cousins puts Vikings in driver's seat to win the division. 

 Cronin: Not real. Cousins' first two games leave little room for an offense adjusting to a new quarterback. Minnesota faces Green Bay at Lambeau Field in Week 10 and then NFC-leading San Francisco in Mexico City. The stretch of Atlanta, Carolina, Detroit and Washington at home is where the Vikings have the best chance to add to their six wins, but two others in the NFC North -- Chicago, with the most complete team, and Detroit, who has the No. 5 scoring offense (27.8 PPG) -- have a better shot at the division title.

 

 Woodyard: Not real. Although Cousins should be an upgrade to the quarterback room, this doesn't immediately fix everything that's wrong with the offense -- or team. Entering Week 10, the Vikings have the NFL's second-worst offensive efficiency (23.77) and Cousins isn't necessarily in the prime of his career at 38, but he does have familiarity in their offensive system and should stabilize the unit enough to compete for a division title.

 Seifert: Not real. It's just too early to say that Cousins can, on his own, lift an offense that ranks No. 31 in EPA enough to ensure superiority over the rest of the division. The truth is quarterback hasn't been only issue. Playcalling, run-game efficiency and, at times, pass protection, have all played roles.

 Demovsky: Not real. In any other division, perhaps a quarterback change of this magnitude on a team that has the No. 2-ranked defense in the NFL would tip the scales in its favor. That doesn't mean Cousins won't help the offense reverse course toward respectability, but it was only a matter of time before this punchless offense made water find its level with the Vikings.

 
 

 Real or not: Caleb Williams ' four picks Sunday were a blip on his way to MVP. 
 Cronin: Not real. The interceptions themselves are a blip, as Williams had the fourth-lowest interception rate (0.6) entering Week 9. Only the first of the four picks were problematic, with Williams admitting he got "greedy" trying to fit a tight-window ball at the goal line. His MVP case needed to be built off peak efficiency to make up for the three games he missed with his hamstring injury, and it's hard to envision him now catching up with the Joe Burrow and Josh Allen at the top of the leaderboard.

 

 Demovsky: Real. I'm going to give him a pass for several reasons: He played mostly interception-free before Sunday against Tampa, one of his interceptions was clearly the fault of receiver Luther Burden III because it bounced off his hands and two others were the result of heavy pressure. The biggest thing working against his MVP case might be his three-game absence.

 Woodyard: Not real.  Williams is certainly a worthy candidate but might not even be the MVP of the NFC North with the way that Packers QB Jordan Love has also been playing -- and without missing any games. Obviously the four interceptions are an anomaly, but he will have to beat out some strong candidates with more efficient play to separate himself.

 Seifert: Not real. I think the Bears are the best team in the division, and Williams has a lot to do with that. The quarterback of a top NFL team is a natural candidate for MVP. But his four-interception game was a byproduct of the way he plays -- aggressively downfield and extending plays outside the pocket. Burrow,  Brock Purdy and Allen are stronger MVP candidates.

 

 

 Real or not: Micah Parsons ' eventual return  to the Packers will be the biggest addition for any NFC North team. 
 Cronin: Not real. Jeffery Simmons would like a word given how quickly he elevated the floor of the Bears' defense upon his arrival in Week 8. Chicago went from blitzing at the fifth-highest rate (42%) prior to the All-Pro defensive tackle's arrival to being able to win with a standard pass rush more frequently. Parsons has not played since Dec. 14, 2025 and will take time to ramp up to his best form. Meanwhile, Simmons' on-field impact is only getting stronger after he logged 87% of snaps in his debut and 97% of snaps in Week 9.

 

 Woodyard: Real. Parsons is a legitimate game-changer and will immediately raise the floor for Green Bay's defense. At his best, there's no question that he's one of the top defensive players in the league, but the question is how long it'll take him to get back to full speed after returning from his ACL injury.

 Seifert: Real. While it might take Parsons some time to ramp up to full strength from a conditioning standpoint, he is the NFL's best pass rusher and that alone will change how every team approaches games against the Packers. The threat alone of his presence, and the need to track wherever he is on the field, is a huge lift for the defense.

 Demovsky: Real. While the Packers didn't make any moves at the trade deadline, Parsons' return (likely on Thanksgiving eve at the Rams) trumps the Bears' trade for Simmons. Parsons has taken extra time to rehab because he wants to be as close to 100% as possible, giving him a better chance to make an immediate impact. As good a job as new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has done without Parsons, he admitted recently that he thinks about what he'll be able to do with Parsons "every day."

 

 

 Real or not: The most overlooked storyline is the  Lions' defensive improvement. 
 Cronin: Real. Kelvin Sheppard's unit deserves a lot of credit for holding the Packers and Vikings (with differing levels of QB play) to 17 and 15 points in back-to-back weeks while allowing fewer than 20 points in three straight games. What stands out most is Detroit being one of 11 teams to hold opponents under 100 rushing yards in every game this season.

 

 Woodyard: Real. After the 32-26 Week 4 loss in Carolina, Sheppard was under heavy fire -- and rightfully so -- when the defense allowed at least 30 or more points in three of its first four games for the first time since the infamous 0-16 season in 2008. title: NFL execs on tight playoff races, MVP, Super Bowl picks, breakouts, more
summary: Who will win the most competitive divisions, and who's in line for awards? We asked sources around the NFL at midseason.
full_text:
The first nine weeks of the NFL season serve as a roadmap for the rest of the season -- complete with a few potholes on the way to Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles.

 The NFC South is usually a rough ride (one your navigation system of choice probably will avoid), and this season is no different. The division is a combined 12-22. The Jacksonville Jaguars have a clear path to L.A., as their AFC South rivals appear low on gas. Jacksonville is 6-2; The rest of the division is 6-19.The Buffalo Bills , at 7-1, are outdistancing the AFC East pit crew, and the NFC East features the New York Giants in cruise control, as the only team with more than four wins.

 But the other four divisions are well-stocked with upgrades -- and enough horsepower to reach L.A. The race begins in earnest now.

 To examine all of this -- as well as identify a few sleepers, MVP options and Super Bowl contenders -- we asked league evaluators to assess the midway point and what happens next in the division races. Buckle up.

 

 
 Jump to exec intel on: 
 NFC North | AFC West 
 NFC West | AFC North 
 Playoff sleepers  | MVP 
 Breakouts | Super Bowl 

 
 

 

 The (NFC) North remembears 
 A division is truly deep when 6-2 gets a team zero separation in the standings. The division is a combined 31-9 entering Week 10, and ESPN's Bill Barnwell made the case it could be the strongest division we've ever seen.

 

 The 6-3 Green Bay Packers have the worst record, but are surging with one of the league's most dangerous passing games. The Vikings' recent addition of Kirk Cousins to complement an elite defense makes that two-game losing streak to fall to 6-2 a little less stressful for Skol faithful. The Detroit Lions can score on any defense, and in several different ways. But it's the man who once led the Detroit offense, Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson, who's considered a separator.

 "Chicago is the best-coached," an AFC executive said. "He's elite. One of the best in the NFL and only in Year 2. One of the best offenses week-in and week-out, as well. Defense is solid. Caleb [Williams] just has to play within the scheme and they will win it easily, I believe."

 Chicago needs its defensive backfield to hold up; the Bears evaluated corner options at the trade deadline before ultimately letting the addition of superstar defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons suffice.

 

 
 

 K.C., Denver on full display 
 The Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs are shaping up for the best two-team divisional race.

 Denver needed every second on the clock to edge Kansas City 28-24 in Week 8. The Chiefs, once winners of nine consecutive AFC West titles, find themselves in the unfamiliar position of chasing a defending champion. But some around the league remain hesitant to pick Denver to win the West for a second consecutive year.

 "They are close enough, but if both teams are healthy, [Patrick] Mahomes gives K.C. the edge," a veteran AFC personnel evaluator said. "Both teams are really good and balanced, so QB play breaks the tie. I still worry about Kansas City's receiving corps, but Denver's offense has been disjointed this year."

 Denver ranks 27th in rushing (91.4 yards per game) and 24th in passing (185.9 yards per game). It's hard to win a divisional title that way, no matter how clutch the defense and Bo Nix are week after week.

 

 
 

 Is the NFC West as advertised? 
 The standings say it's not. Very few people projected the two teams in last year's NFC Championship Game to have matching 5-4 records at this stage, but that's exactly where the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams sit.

 

 Both teams have problems: Seattle is struggling to score, and the Rams can't get healthy. Regardless, both teams might just be talented enough to make a run at San Francisco (7-1), which hosts the Seahawks in Week 12 and the Rams in Week 14. The 49ers look like a team ready to wrap up the division by then.

 "They've already built a [2½-game] lead and it looks like they are turning the corner on injuries," an AFC executive said. "The Rams didn't get a receiver at the deadline and that's going to hurt. [Seahawks quarteback]  Sam Darnold is struggling in the new offense and Arizona is, well, Arizona."

 Most of San Francisco's starting defense has returned, and receivers Mike Evans and  Deebo Samuel Sr . will be back soon enough. Meanwhile, Los Angeles is without Davante Adams and Puka Nacua , and Darnold is missing a stretch of games for the second time this season.

 

 
 

 Depth prevails in AFC North 
 The AFC North is one (OK, two) Lamar Jackson injuries away from rivaling its NFC parallel as the deepest division in football.

 Jackson's absence has Baltimore reeling, but the Steelers are riding a four-game winning streak and the Bengals just poured 143 points on their past four opponents. Cleveland, despite a two-game losing streak, has a lot of optimism, as the Browns are brimming with young talent. 

 In the eyes of many evaluators, though, the Bengals are poised to win their first divisional crown since 2022, if health prevails and the defense holds up.

 "I'm going with the Bengals because of Burrow," an NFC executive said. "He's playing at such a high level, and even though they struggle to run the ball at times, it almost doesn't matter because of all that he does. If the defense can just maintain, they should be a threat."

 Evaluators note the Steelers' offensive line and running backs are playing very well (Jaylen Warren's 5.9 yards per carry leads all qualified players by a healthy margin), but many still don't trust the passing game enough to knock off Cincinnati.

 

 
 

 Two sleepers who could wake up 
 Those who picked the  Houston Texans  to make a deep playoff push are clinging to those projections despite the Texans' disappointing 3-5 clip.

 "[C.J.] Stroud is playing really well, and there's reason to believe the defense will round into form in the second half," an AFC scout said. "The running game has been hit or miss but that's been the case."

 The 3-6  Tampa Bay Buccaneers  could make some noise if they emerge from the NFC South race. A stout defense and potent running game should translate well to January football.

 

 
 

 Brock Purdy: From Mr. Irrelevant to MVP? 
 Brock Purdy  and Joe Burrow got the most consideration here, but Purdy is leading the best team and has the highest QBR at 81.4. He's also on pace to rush for more than 400 yards.

 

 "He's playing a position at a high level, "an NFC executive said. "He's putting it all together."

 Another NFL executive who named Purdy cited another reason he could prevail. "It's a narrative-driven award and they look like the best team in the NFC, he's playing efficiently and they haven't been healthy so he is helping lift them up." 

 Burrow is in the midst of his best season and leads the league in touchdowns. C.J. Stroud has also taken a leap in Houston, positioning himself for a huge contract this offseason, and  Jordan Love is keeping the Packers in contention despite a highly questionable offensive line.

 

 

 

 Ascending rookies 
 Running back Kaelon Black looks the part in Kyle Shanahan's 49ers offense, with 23 carries for 133 yards and a touchdown in his past two games. That profile could only grow.

 "He's an explosive runner who's hard to keep off the field, and Christian [McCaffrey] will undoubtedly get hurt at some point," an NFC exec said.

 On defense, evaluators are watching Kansas City's R Mason Thomas closely. The second-round pick has only one sack but untapped potential with impressive get-off. "It's a matter of time for him," an NFC scout said.

 

 
 

 Super Bowl picks to keep an eye on 
 Look out for this matchup: The  Chicago Bears  against the  Buffalo Bills . Both teams have multifaceted offensive attacks, star quarterbacks with dual-threat ability and enough roster talent to get hot.

 

 We touched on Chicago earlier. As for Buffalo, it features "the best quarterback and offense by far," as one AFC…

title: Travis Hunter makes Jessie Bates' Jaguars trade a hit with his nephews
summary: The safety's young nephews were thrilled to learn their uncle would be Hunter's teammate.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Safety Jessie Bates III said Thursday that he's excited about joining the Jacksonville Jaguars for the rest of the season. But not, apparently, as excited as his nephews.

 

 Mostly because their uncle is now teammates with Travis Hunter . The Jaguars posted a video of Bates' ride to the team's facility Monday after being acquired in a trade with the Atlanta Falcons , and during the drive Bates took a FaceTime call from one of his nephews, who said, "You finally get to work with Travis Hunter."

 Wait until they find out Bates' locker is next to Hunter's.

 "I don't know if my nephews will be more excited," Bates joked. "I don't know if you guys have seen that video, but I don't think they care that I'm here. I think they're happy I'm just here with Travis.

 

 "My nephews, they're 10 and 7, and you'd think that they're 21 years old the way they know how to work the internet and just their knowledge of the game itself. It's really cool to see. And yeah, they'll be excited when they get down here in a couple weeks."

 Hunter smiled when asked about the video Thursday and said he would make sure he got Bates' nephews a jersey.

title: Fernando Mendoza and the Raiders' sit-and-learn plan: Is he ready to start?
summary: The Raiders had a plan for Fernando Mendoza in Year 1 and stuck to it as long as they could. But he's now QB1 earlier than expected, and they have to trust he's ready.
full_text:
The day you find out you're going to be a parent is one of the scariest days of your life. It comes with all the worries, from the mundane and practical (What if I drop him?) to the broad and existential (What if I mess him up?). All of it comes under the terrifying umbrella of "What if I'm not ready?"

 The fact is you're probably not, and you probably never will be.

 This thought popped into my head Tuesday, when the Raiders' deadline-day trade of Kirk Cousins to the Vikings suddenly elevated rookie Fernando Mendoza  into the role of starting quarterback -- sooner than the team had planned. Is he ready? Maybe not, but that's not the relevant question anymore. It's happening, and all the Raiders can do is try their best to not mess this up.

 "It shouldn't be a whirlwind if he's been preparing the right way each week," Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said Thursday. "At some point, he knew he was going to get an opportunity, and so he's been preparing that way since April."

 

 Sure, sounds great. Mendoza was the first pick in the 2026 draft as a Heisman Trophy winner and national champion. He's comfortable in the spotlight and has a history of exceeding expectations. He might be absolutely fine from the jump. He might have been fine if the Raiders had never signed Cousins and they had started him in Week 1, the way the Titans did with Cam Ward last season, the Bears did with Caleb Williams the year before that, the Panthers did with Bryce Young the year before that, and so on. All of those guys had plenty of hiccups at the start -- there aren't a lot of Joe Burrow s or Andrew Lucks out there who get picked No. 1 and hit right away -- but there's also no real evidence that starting right away is the reason Young and Ward are still struggling, or that Williams is lighting up the league in Year 3.

 The Raiders were extremely intentional about this. Once they knew they had the first pick and were taking Mendoza there, they made an intricate plan.

 First, they hired an offensive-minded head coach who had just won the Super Bowl as Sam Darnold 's offensive coordinator and has a history of scheming things up to put quarterbacks of varying ability levels in positions to succeed. They told anyone who'd listen that they absolutely did not want to play Mendoza right away. Raiders minority owner Tom Brady has been vocal about his belief that rookie quarterbacks need more time to develop than the NFL tends to give them, and Brady's voice carries a great deal of weight in that building right now. The Raiders have said since the offseason that they wanted to make sure not only that Mendoza was ready, but also that they were ready for him. In other words, they wanted to give the roster enough time to develop so they didn't have to ask him to carry it once the time came.

 To that end, Las Vegas signed Cousins in free agency and made it clear at every step that he was going to be the starter. The Raiders built out an offensive coaching staff designed to give Mendoza whatever he needed. Kubiak was the game-plan guru and overall organizational tone-setter. And former Seattle assistant Andrew Janocko, who has now worked on the same staff as Kubiak for five of the past seven years, was hired as the coordinator.

 Longtime NFL coach Mike Sullivan was brought on as quarterbacks coach, a role in which he has been assigned as direct overseer of Mendoza's development. Sources with knowledge of the situation say Sullivan's involvement with Cousins and the day-to-day prep work for the games has been minimal compared to his direct coaching of Mendoza. He was hired to get the first overall pick ready.

 Sullivan has seen this before. He was on the Giants' coaching staff in 2004, when New York landed Eli Manning and had him sit behind veteran Kurt Warner for the first nine games of his first season before having the rookie start the final seven contests. This situation is eerily similar to that one. Those Giants were 5-4 when they switched from Warner to Manning. These Raiders are 4-5.

 

 I remember asking Manning years ago about his philosophy on rookie quarterbacks sitting or playing right away. He told me he felt he'd had the best of both worlds -- the chance to sit and learn from Warner while getting his feet wet as a professional, along with the chance to start a meaningful number of games as a rookie so his head wasn't spinning when he opened the 2005 season as the starter. (David Carr was Manning's backup at the time of this conversation, and he told me he wished he'd had the chance to sit behind a veteran himself, instead of starting right away as a rookie in Houston in 2002.)

 Mendoza is already feeling what Manning felt. At his news conference Wednesday , he expressed heartfelt gratitude for Cousins, whom he said "had me with open arms and has taught me so many things, whether it's film study, how to operate as a starting quarterback, all the different multifaceted approaches that have made him so successful, he has shared with no restrictions or constraints."

 The Raiders' hope was for that to continue. As recently as last weekend, there were people in that organization who wanted to stick to the plan -- to keep Cousins past the trade deadline and hold off on playing Mendoza a few more weeks, maybe even until after their Week 13 bye. The Vikings called the Raiders about Cousins prior to last weekend, but it wasn't until after Sunday that they felt there was a chance Vegas would trade him.

 Tuesday's trade deadline -- and a disastrous performance by Carson Wentz for the Vikings on Monday night -- sped up both teams' timetables. If the deadline were two weeks from now, it's entirely possible the Vikings wouldn't have offered a third-round pick for Cousins quite yet, or that the Raiders wouldn't have listened anyway. But life doesn't wait to see how your plans are going. Sometimes, it forces you to do something before you're sure you're ready to do it.

 What the Raiders did here is rare. From 2006 to 2025, there were 41 quarterbacks selected in the top 10 overall. Of those 41, only six did not start at least one of their teams' first eight games in their respective rookie seasons, per ESPN Research. And only two of those six -- JaMarcus Russell and Jared Goff -- were picked first overall. The others were Jake Locker, Patrick Mahomes , Michael Penix Jr . and J.J. McCarthy . That's a pretty wide range of outcomes, and it shows why there's no set playbook for how to do this.

 The ideal path is the 2017 Chiefs, who drafted Mahomes to sit behind Alex Smith, started 5-0, stayed in first place all season and only started Mahomes in the final regular-season game because they had their playoff seed locked up. No one else has really been able to pull that off. (Yes,  Jordan Love was a first-rounder who got to sit for three years, but that was because  Aaron Rodgers was still in Green Bay winning MVP awards.)

 

 In 2024, the Patriots tried to sit Drake Maye behind an ineffective Jacoby Brissett , then started Maye in Week 6 only to find out he had been ready all along. That same year, the Commanders started Jayden Daniels right away and ended up in the NFC Championship Game, the Broncos started  Bo Nix  right away and made the playoffs, the Falcons kept Penix on the bench (behind Cousins) for 14 games and still aren't sure what they have there, and the Vikings didn't play McCarthy because he got hurt in August . In 2023, the Texans started C.J. Stroud right away, and he won Rookie of the Year. The Colts started Anthony Richardson Sr . right away that same year to disastrous results whose effects the organization still feels three years later.

 Justin Herbert had to start the second game of his 2020 rookie season on a couple of minutes' notice after a team doctor injured Tyrod Taylor  while giving him a pregame injection. Jaxson Dart had to go in earlier than planned for the Giants last season because Russell Wilson was terrible and then-coach Brian Daboll had (justified,…

title: Commanders keep NFC East hopes alive with win over Giants
summary: New York couldn't close out a win against Washington, giving up a late touchdown drive. Its division lead is now shrinking.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The Washington Commanders might have saved their season Thursday night. If nothing else, the Commanders extended the belief that they can contend for the NFC East title.

 Washington's comeback 24-21 win against the New York Giants improved its record to 3-5-1. Now, the Commanders are two games behind New York while owning the tiebreaker. They have more work to do to climb back into the race, but the win staved off questions about Dan Quinn's coaching future.

 If they had lost Thursday, they would have been all but eliminated -- and Quinn's job security would have become a primary topic considering they entered the game 7-17-1 since the start of last season. It was the first time Washington won by scoring a touchdown on its final drive. The Commanders had been 1-3-1 in games decided by a touchdown or less before Thursday.

 Here are the most important things to know for both teams:

 

 

 

 Washington Commanders  (3-5-1) 
 What to make of Daniels' performance: Jayden Daniels overcame his first two interceptions of the season and delivered when Washington needed him most. His strength has been shaking off bad plays, and after consecutive series ended with picks in the fourth quarter, he led the go-ahead touchdown drive -- with a 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs . Daniels had been highly efficient prior to that pass. He has gotten better at keeping his eyes downfield, which resulted in one play for 30 yards.

 Trend to watch: Washington's defense has forced six turnovers in its past three games combined. The Commanders now have 14 takeaways this season, but none was bigger than corner Rasul Douglas ' interception to end the Giants' final possession. Washington forced a fumble in the red zone, preventing a potential field goal if nothing else.

 Most surprising performance: Tight end Ben Sinnott . He entered with one reception on the season, a disappointing total for the 2024 second-round pick. He was supposed to get more action in Washington's new scheme this season, but it took until Week 10 for him to play a bigger role. He caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown against the Giants. -- Keim 

 Next game: vs. Cincinnati Bengals (Nov. 23, at 8:15 p.m. ET)

 

 

 

 New York Giants  (5-3-1) 
 The Giants had a chance to all but bury the NFC East by beating the Commanders. They came up just short by allowing Washington to go 71 yards in 49 seconds late in the fourth quarter and throwing a late interception that ended the game. Now, the division is back open.

 The Commanders have life. The door is open for the Dallas Cowboys , who play the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. The Giants entered Thursday night with a 2.5-game lead in the division. A victory would have made them 3-0-1 with wins over each team in the division. They just couldn't finish this one, even with quarterback J.J. McCarthy playing one of the best games of his career up until coming up short in the final seconds.

 What to make of McCarthy's performance:  Another strong performance by McCarthy, although it was muddied by the game-ending interception with 25 seconds remaining. He completed 23 of 36 passes for a career-high 293 yards with one touchdown and one interception. The touchdown pass was an impressive strike on third down with a defender in his face, a 66-yard score to tight end Isaiah Likely that gave the Giants the lead in the fourth quarter.

 McCarthy was also able to use his legs in this contest. The mobile quarterback rushed for 34 yards as the Giants' offense ran some of the stuff it originally had in the playbook for Jaxson Dart . His play remains promising despite the loss.

 Trend to watch:  Cam Skattebo thrives in primetime games. The second-year running back said this week that the best players show up when the lights are on. Well, Skattebo now has two games in his career with multiple touchdowns on the ground. Both were on a Thursday night. He rushed for three TDs in Week 6 in 2025 as a rookie against the Philadelphia Eagles and two Thursday against the Commanders.

 Surprising performance: Safety  Ar'Darius Washington . He made three massive plays: an interception in the flat with 2:15 remaining, a forced turnover on downs early in the fourth quarter and a good tackle in the open field on Chig Okonkwo on third down. Then he knocked down a pass meant for Diggs that set up the Giants for a touchdown. 

 Stat to know: The Giants' 16-play touchdown   drive in the first half was their longest since Week 9 in 2024. It culminated with a 1-yard touchdown run for Skattebo. The Giants converted two third downs and one fourth down on their seven-minute, 48-second march into the end zone to take the lead in the first half. The Giants had two TD drives (against Houston and Philadelphia) of 14 plays.  -- Raanan 

 Next game: vs. Jacksonville Jaguars (Nov. 22, at 4:25 p.m. ET)
